##### @spec a-rule-over-every-thing-of-a-kind-says-a-noun-in-its-when

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says a "for every" as the rule it holds, where that rule has no "otherwise". Its first side says "a" and the noun of each variable: "when a cleanup has run, code has registered the cleanup". Over two variables it says "when a cleanup is on an owner and pulse has disposed the owner, the cleanup has run".

This follows because English states a rule over a kind this way, and the words keep the meaning the "for every" gave them.

##### @spec a-definition-of-every-thing-of-a-kind-says-a-noun-as-its-subject

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says a [*definition*](#term-definition-passage) over one parameter as its words alone, where they open with the parameter. Their subject is "a" and the noun: "a unit is unfounded exactly when the unit is one of these".

This follows because a definition says what a word means of any one thing of its kind. "A unit is … exactly when …" says that the way a glossary does.

##### @spec a-variable-named-once-keeps-its-for-every

> Where the words name the variable of a "for every" only once, the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) keeps the "for every".

This follows because "a bug" with no "the bug" after it could mean some bug or every bug. Only every bug is what the formula says.

##### @spec a-rule-with-an-otherwise-keeps-its-for-every

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) keeps the "for every" of a rule that has an "otherwise".

This follows because the "otherwise" speaks of the things for which the first side does not hold. A reader who took "a bug" in the first side as some bug would read the "otherwise" as the case where no bug does.

#### @spec a-variable-is-named-the-same-however-the-formula-names-it

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) names the variables the same way, whatever names the [*formula*](#term-formula) gives them.

This follows because the name the author chose says nothing about the logic, and a statement must not change when the author renames a variable.

#### @spec some-is-said-with-an-article-chosen-by-the-sound-of-the-noun

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `some` of a type with the article "a" or "an" that fits the sound of the noun.

This follows because English picks the article from the sound of the noun, and a reader notices a wrong one.

#### @spec an-article-the-noun-is-written-with-wins-over-its-sound

> When the noun of a type carries an article, the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) uses that article, whatever the sound of the noun.

This follows because the author knows the word better than the sound rule, and an hour is an hour.

#### @spec no-over-several-variables-is-said-as-no-combination

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `no` over variables of several types as no combination of the variables.

This follows because a statement that none of each variable exists would mean something else than none of them together.

#### @spec one-as-a-quantifier-is-said-as-exactly-one

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `one` over a variable as "exactly one" of its noun, and over several variables as exactly one combination of them.

This follows because `one` holds when the body holds for one value of the variables and for no other. Over several variables, the value is the combination.

#### @spec lone-as-a-quantifier-is-said-as-at-most-one

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `lone` over a variable as "at most one" of its noun, and over several variables as at most one combination of them.

This follows because `lone` holds when the body holds for no value of the variables or for one.

#### @spec a-block-as-the-body-of-a-quantifier-is-said-as-its-formulas-together

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says a [*quantifier*](#term-quantifier) whose body is a block, `all x: T { a b }`, as the quantifier with the formulas of the block holding together.

This follows because the formulas of a block hold together, as if `and` joined them.

#### @spec a-call-of-a-predicate-gives-its-variables-numbers-that-are-free

> When a called body quantifies a variable that the [*call*](#term-predicate-call) already uses, the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) gives it a number that no variable in use has.

This follows because a reader takes two variables with one name for one variable, and the statement would say what the logic does not.

#### @spec a-variable-of-a-body-never-takes-the-name-of-an-argument

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) never gives a variable of a called body the name of an argument of the [*call*](#term-predicate-call).

This follows because the argument and the variable would read as one thing.

#### @spec the-alternatives-of-a-list-reuse-a-name-and-keep-it-taken-for-what-follows

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) gives the same name to the variable in each alternative of a [*list*](#term-series), and keeps the name taken for what follows.

This follows because alternatives do not hold together, so one name in each is clear. What follows must not reuse a name an alternative took.

#### @spec the-statements-of-a-list-each-use-the-same-names

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) uses the same names in each statement of a [*list*](#term-series) that quantifies a variable of one type. A time phrase before the statement, such as "from now on", changes nothing.

This follows because statements of a list stand apart, and a reader reads each from its own start.

#### @spec conditions-that-hold-together-keep-their-names-apart

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) gives a different name to the variable of each condition in a [*list*](#term-series) of conditions that hold together.

This follows because conditions that hold together may talk about the same thing, and one name would join what the logic keeps apart.

#### @spec a-predicate-with-no-reading-is-said-by-its-body

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says a [*call*](#term-predicate-call) of a predicate with no reading by its body, with each argument in the place it fills.

This follows because the author gave the predicate a body so that it means something, and the body is the next best words.

#### @spec a-negated-predicate-with-no-reading-is-said-as-untrue

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says a negated [*call*](#term-predicate-call) of a predicate with no reading as "it is not the case that", followed by the body. It sets a body that is more than one plain clause apart below those words.

This follows because the negative of a body has no words of its own, so the sentence says that the body does not hold. Before a body of two clauses on the same line, a reader could take the "not" as covering only the first.

#### @spec the-reading-of-the-table-wins-over-the-body

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says a [*call*](#term-predicate-call) of a predicate that has both a reading and a body with the reading.

This follows because the table is where the author says how a word sounds, and the body is a fallback.

#### @spec the-checker-reads-the-predicates-a-vocabulary-declares

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) reads each predicate that a vocabulary declares: its name, what it takes and its body.

This follows because the verbalizer can use only the body of a predicate that has no reading, and the body lives in the vocabulary.

#### @spec a-call-written-as-a-join-is-said-as-the-call

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `x.p` and `x.p[y]`, for a predicate `p`, as `p[x]` and `p[x, y]`.

This follows because Alloy reads a join with a predicate as a call with the left side as its first argument.

#### @spec a-box-join-of-a-field-is-said-as-the-navigation

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `f[x]`, for a field `f`, as `x.f`.

This follows because Alloy reads `f[x]` as the join `x.f`.

#### @spec a-call-with-an-expression-is-said-by-the-body-with-the-expression-in-place

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says a [*call*](#term-predicate-call) of a predicate with no reading by its body also when an argument is an expression. The expression takes the place of the parameter.

Derives from: [`spec-a-predicate-with-no-reading-is-said-by-its-body`](#spec-a-predicate-with-no-reading-is-said-by-its-body)

This follows because Alloy binds the parameter to the value of the expression, whatever it holds.

#### @spec a-call-with-one-value-is-said-through-a-member-in-the-place-of-the-argument

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says a [*call*](#term-predicate-call) of a predicate with a reading and an argument of one value through a member of its type. That member is the one in the argument.

This follows because an argument that holds exactly one value is that value, and the reading says something of one thing in each slot. The declarations make a navigation of `one` fields from a variable one value.

#### @spec a-call-with-an-argument-of-none-or-several-values-is-refused

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses a [*call*](#term-predicate-call) of a predicate with a reading, with an argument that can hold none or several values, and names the argument.

This follows because the reading says something of one thing, and the predicate gets every value of the argument at once.

#### @spec a-call-with-an-argument-of-another-type-is-refused

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses a [*call*](#term-predicate-call) whose argument is of a type that shares no member with the type of its parameter, and names both types.

This follows because Alloy rejects such a call as a type error, so the formula claims nothing. Words for it would claim something.

#### @spec a-let-is-said-with-its-value-in-the-place-of-its-name

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `let x = e | f` as `f` with `e` in the place of `x`. A `let` of several names puts each value in place, in order.

This follows because a `let` only names a value, and the formula it holds means what it means with the value written out.

#### @spec a-let-whose-value-a-quantifier-of-its-body-would-capture-is-refused

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses a `let` whose body declares a variable with a name that its value uses, and names the variable.

Derives from: [`spec-a-let-is-said-with-its-value-in-the-place-of-its-name`](#spec-a-let-is-said-with-its-value-in-the-place-of-its-name)

This follows because the value put in place would then name the variable of the body, where the `let` names another thing.

#### @spec a-negation-is-said-with-the-negative-reading-of-what-it-negates

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says the negation of a comparison or a [*call*](#term-predicate-call) with the negative reading of what it negates.

This follows because the table gives each word a positive and a negative reading so that no sentence needs a clumsy "not".

#### @spec not-before-a-compound-is-said-with-the-not-moved-inward

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `not` before a [*list*](#term-series), a rule, an equivalence, a [*quantifier*](#term-quantifier) or a temporal operator as the [*formula*](#term-formula) it equals with the `not` moved inward. Where no such formula exists, it says "it is not the case that" before the formula, set apart.

This follows because the negative reading of each clause says the negation in the words of the table. Moving the `not` inward reaches those clauses without changing what the formula claims.

<!-- pass-negation-inward:begin — generated by `node test/core/wordings.ts --write`; edits are overwritten -->
The pass `negation-inward` is pass 1 of 25 in the pipeline. It changes 115 of the 1776 formulas of the sweep.

The shortest of them, as written in Alloy:

```text
all c: Cleanup, s: String | c.tags not in "a"
```

Without the pass:

```text
For every cleanup and every text T1:
  it is not the case that:
    for every text T2:
      when the cleanup is tagged text T2, text T2 and "a" are the same.
```

With it:

```text
For every cleanup and every text:
  the cleanup is tagged a text other than "a".
```
<!-- pass-negation-inward:end -->

##### @spec not-before-an-and-is-said-as-at-least-one-negation

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `not (a and b)` as `not a or not b`.

This follows because a run of clauses fails exactly when one of them fails.

##### @spec not-before-an-or-is-said-as-every-negation

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `not (a or b)` as `not a and not b`.

This follows because a run of alternatives fails exactly when each of them fails.

##### @spec not-before-a-rule-is-said-as-its-condition-and-the-negation-of-its-consequence

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `not (a implies b)` as `a and not b`.

This follows because a rule fails exactly when its condition holds and its consequence does not.

##### @spec not-before-an-equivalence-is-said-as-exactly-one-of-its-sides

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `not (a iff b)` as exactly one of `a` and `b` holding.

This follows because an equivalence fails exactly when one side holds and the other does not.

<!-- pass-exactly-one:begin — generated by `node test/core/wordings.ts --write`; edits are overwritten -->
The pass `exactly-one` is pass 2 of 25 in the pipeline. It changes 30 of the 1776 formulas of the sweep.

The shortest of them, as written in Alloy:

```text
all c: Cleanup, o, p: Owner | not (c in Ran iff o in Disposed)
```

Without the pass:

```text
For every cleanup, every owner O1 and every owner O2:
  it is not the case that:
    the cleanup has run exactly when pulse has disposed owner O1.
```

With it:

```text
For every cleanup, every owner O1 and every owner O2:
  exactly one of these holds:
    - the cleanup has run
    - pulse has disposed owner O1
```
<!-- pass-exactly-one:end -->

##### @spec not-before-an-else-is-said-as-the-rule-with-each-side-negated

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `not (c implies a else b)` as `c implies not a else not b`.

This follows because the condition picks one side, and the negation fails the side it picks.

##### @spec not-before-some-or-no-is-said-as-the-other

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `not some x: T | f` as `no x: T | f`, and `not no x: T | f` as `some x: T | f`.

This follows because `no` is the negation of `some`.

##### @spec not-before-all-is-said-as-some-with-the-body-negated

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `not all x: T | f` as `some x: T | not f`.

This follows because a claim about every value fails exactly when it fails for one.

##### @spec not-before-always-or-eventually-is-said-as-the-other-with-the-formula-negated

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `not always f` as `eventually not f`, and `not eventually f` as `always not f`.

This follows because a claim about every later moment fails exactly when it fails at one of them.

##### @spec not-before-historically-or-once-is-said-as-the-other-with-the-formula-negated

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `not historically f` as `once not f`, and `not once f` as `historically not f`.

This follows because the past operators mirror the future ones.

##### @spec not-before-after-is-said-as-after-with-the-formula-negated

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `not after f` as `after not f`.

Derives from: [`fact-every-moment-has-a-next-moment`](#fact-every-moment-has-a-next-moment)

This follows because each moment has exactly one next moment, so `f` fails there exactly when `not f` holds there.

##### @spec a-not-with-no-formula-to-move-into-is-said-as-it-is-not-the-case-that

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `not` before `one`, `lone`, `before` or a binary temporal operator as "it is not the case that", with the [*formula*](#term-formula) it negates set apart below it.

This follows because none of these has a negation the words say more simply. Setting the formula apart shows where the negation ends.

#### @spec a-union-on-the-left-is-spelled-out

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says a comparison with a union on its left as one statement for each member of the union. For `in` each statement holds, and for `not in` at least one fails.

This follows because a comparison with a union says it of each member, and the reader should not have to unfold it.

With `not in`, the formula denies that every member is in the set, so one member outside it is enough.

#### @spec a-difference-on-the-right-is-spelled-out

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says a comparison with a difference on its right as: the left side is in the first part and not in the second.

This follows because a difference says the right side holds and the removed part does not, which is two statements.

#### @spec a-disj-quantifier-is-said-with-its-variables-different

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says a [*quantifier*](#term-quantifier) with `disj` as the same quantifier with the condition that its variables are different.

This follows because `disj` says that the variables of one declaration stand for different things, and nothing more.

#### @spec a-difference-as-the-type-of-a-quantifier-is-said-as-a-condition

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says a [*quantifier*](#term-quantifier) over `A - B` as a quantifier over `A`, with the condition that the variable is not in `B`. When `B` is a variable, the condition is that the two are different.

This follows because the variable ranges over the members of `A` that are not in `B`, which is the type and the condition together.

#### @spec a-set-with-no-noun-as-the-type-of-a-quantifier-is-said-as-a-condition

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says a [*quantifier*](#term-quantifier) over a set `S` with no noun over the signature that holds `S`, with the condition that the variable is in `S`.

Derives from: [`spec-some-or-no-of-a-set-of-things-is-said-as-a-noun-phrase-of-its-signature`](#spec-some-or-no-of-a-set-of-things-is-said-as-a-noun-phrase-of-its-signature)

This follows because each member of `S` is a member of the signature that holds it. The variable ranges over the members of that signature that are in `S`.

#### @spec an-expression-as-the-type-of-a-quantifier-is-said-as-a-condition

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says a [*quantifier*](#term-quantifier) over an expression `e`, such as `all o: c.on | …`, as one over the type of `e`, with the condition that the variable is in `e`.

Derives from: [`spec-a-set-with-no-noun-as-the-type-of-a-quantifier-is-said-as-a-condition`](#spec-a-set-with-no-noun-as-the-type-of-a-quantifier-is-said-as-a-condition)

This follows because the variable ranges over the members of `e`, and each is a member of its type.

#### @spec a-disj-after-the-colon-is-said-as-a-disj-before-the-names

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `x, y: disj T` as it says `disj x, y: T`.

Derives from: [`spec-a-disj-quantifier-is-said-with-its-variables-different`](#spec-a-disj-quantifier-is-said-with-its-variables-different)

This follows because Alloy reads `disj` in either place as the condition that the variables are different.

#### @spec one-before-the-type-of-a-variable-is-said-as-the-type

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `x: one T`, of a [*quantifier*](#term-quantifier) or of a parameter, as `x: T`.

This follows because `one` is what a declaration means when it names no multiplicity: the variable is one member of `T`.

#### @spec a-variable-that-can-hold-several-things-or-none-is-refused

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses a variable declared `lone`, `some` or `set`, or with an arrow in its type, and says that it can hold none or several things.

This follows because a reading says something of one thing in each slot. The readings give no words for "for every" set of things.

#### @spec private-before-a-variable-of-a-quantifier-is-refused

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses `private` before a variable of a [*quantifier*](#term-quantifier), which Alloy does not read.

This follows because the analyzer rejects it, so the formula claims nothing.

#### @spec membership-in-a-navigation-is-said-with-the-reading-of-its-field

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `x in y.f` and `y in f.x` with the reading of the field `f`, with `y` in its first slot and `x` in its second.

This follows because `x in y.f` holds exactly when `y->x` is in `f`, which is what the reading of the field says.

#### @spec no-or-some-of-a-navigation-is-said-as-a-noun-phrase-of-the-type-of-the-field

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `no y.f` and `some y.f` as `no` or `some` of the type that the field `f` points at. The reading of the field puts that noun beside `y`.

This follows because `no y.f` holds exactly when nothing is in `y.f`, and the field declares what can be.

#### @spec a-transpose-in-a-navigation-is-said-as-the-navigation-the-other-way

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `y.~f` as `f.y`, and `~f.y` as `y.f`.

Derives from: [`spec-membership-in-a-navigation-is-said-with-the-reading-of-its-field`](#spec-membership-in-a-navigation-is-said-with-the-reading-of-its-field)

This follows because `~f` holds `x->y` exactly when `f` holds `y->x`. A navigation of `~f` from one side reaches what a navigation of `f` from the other side reaches, and the reading of `f` says that.

#### @spec a-pair-in-a-transpose-is-said-the-other-way-round

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `x->y in ~r` as `y->x in r`.

This follows because `~r` holds `x->y` exactly when `r` holds `y->x`.

#### @spec some-or-no-of-a-set-of-things-is-said-as-a-noun-phrase-of-its-signature

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `some S` and `no S`, for a set `S` whose reading takes a variable, as `some` or `no` of the signature that holds `S`. That signature is the one `S` is declared `in` or `extends`, or `S` itself when it stands on its own.

This follows because `some S` holds exactly when a member of that signature is in `S`, and the reading of `S` says what being in `S` is.

##### @spec a-set-whose-reading-says-its-variable-once-is-said-with-a-noun-phrase-in-its-place

> When the reading of `S` says its variable once, the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) puts a noun phrase of the signature in its place: "an edge is being delivered".

This follows because the phrase names the one member that the reading is about, in the one place the reading says it.

##### @spec a-set-whose-reading-says-its-variable-twice-is-said-in-full

> When the reading of `S` says its variable more than once, the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `some S` and `no S` in full: a [*quantifier*](#term-quantifier) over the signature, with a numbered name.

This follows because a noun phrase in two places would read as two things, where the logic has one.

##### @spec a-set-with-no-one-signature-that-holds-it-is-refused

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses `some S` and `no S`, for a set `S` whose reading takes a variable, when the vocabulary declares no one signature that holds `S`, and names `S`.

This follows because without the signature the verbalizer has no noun for the members of `S`, and any noun it chose would be invented.

#### @spec a-primed-name-with-no-reading-of-its-own-is-said-at-the-next-moment

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says a clause that primes one set or field as "at the next moment" and the clause without the prime. A reading of the primed name wins.

This follows because a variable is the same thing at every moment. The primed name is then the only part of the clause that the next moment changes.

#### @spec two-sets-compared-are-said-member-by-member

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says two sets or two relations compared with `in`, `=` or `!=` member by member, over the types of their columns.

This follows because `Ran in Registered` holds exactly when every member of `Ran` is in `Registered`, and a reading says that of one member at a time. A frame condition such as `Registered' = Registered + c` reads this way too.

#### @spec a-field-of-pairs-has-the-types-of-its-columns

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) takes the types of the columns of a field declared with an arrow from its declaration, as `older: Cleanup -> Cleanup` of `Clock`.

This follows because the verbalizer says a comparison of such a field, such as `Clock.older' = Clock.older`, over its tuples. Without the types of its columns, the verbalizer would refuse it, and every predicate that keeps it unchanged.

#### @spec membership-in-an-else-of-sets-is-said-through-each-branch

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `x in (c implies a else b)` as a rule with an "otherwise": when `c`, `x` is in `a`, and otherwise `x` is in `b`.

This follows because an else of sets is `a` where `c` holds and `b` where it does not.

#### @spec an-integer-in-a-number-is-said-as-equal-to-it

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `y in n`, for a variable `y` that a [*quantifier*](#term-quantifier) declares an integer and a number `n`, as `y = n`.

This follows because a number is one integer, so to be in it is to equal it. Of a variable whose type it does not know, the verbalizer still refuses it.

#### @spec all-or-some-over-a-union-of-signatures-is-said-over-each

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `all`, `some` or `no` of one variable over a union of signatures that no one type holds as the same [*quantifier*](#term-quantifier) over each signature.

This follows because a formula holds for every member of `A + B` exactly when it holds for every member of each. `some` is the same with "or". The verbalizer refuses `one` and `lone` over such a union, because they do not split that way.

#### @spec sides-that-alloy-does-not-compare-are-refused

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses a comparison of sides that hold tuples of different sizes, or things of types that share no member.

This follows because Alloy rejects such a comparison as a type error, so it claims nothing. Words for it would claim something.

#### @spec an-equality-with-a-side-of-unknown-type-is-refused

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses `=` or `!=` between two sets when the vocabulary does not tell the type of a side that is not a variable.

This follows because the words say the equality over the type of a side. Members of the other side outside that type would go unsaid.

#### @spec a-field-of-one-value-equal-to-a-variable-is-said-with-its-reading

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `x.f = y` and `x.f != y`, for a field `f` that the vocabulary declares `one` or `lone`, with the reading of the field.

This follows because a field of at most one value equals `y` exactly when `y` is in it.

#### @spec a-field-of-many-values-equal-to-a-variable-is-said-member-by-member

> Take a field `f` that can hold more than one value, where its reading with `y` is more than one plain clause. The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `x.f = y` member by member. For every member of the type of `f`, it says the reading of `f` "exactly when" the member and `y` are the same. It says `x.f != y` as the negation of that.

This follows because a set equals `y` when `y` is in it and nothing else is. The reading of the field says only the first half. Where the reading is one plain clause, [`spec-a-set-equal-to-a-variable-is-said-as-the-variable-and-no-other`](#spec-a-set-equal-to-a-variable-is-said-as-the-variable-and-no-other) says both halves in a sentence.

#### @spec a-set-equal-to-a-variable-is-said-as-the-variable-and-no-other

> Take a variable `x`, and a set or a field of many values `s`, where being in `s` is one plain clause. The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `s = x` as `x` in `s` "and" no other member of its type in `s`: "the cleanup is on owner_1 and is on no other owner". The second half drops a subject the two share.

This follows because a set equals `x` when `x` is in it and nothing else is, and the two halves say just that. "No other" alone hints that `x` is in the set, which [`spec-no-with-another-is-said-in-full`](#spec-no-with-another-is-said-in-full) guards against. Here the first half says it, so the hint is true. A plain clause keeps "no other" at the level of the claim. Inside a noun phrase, as in "an owner that no other owner is the parent of", it would cover less.

<!-- pass-x-and-no-other:begin — generated by `node test/core/wordings.ts --write`; edits are overwritten -->
The pass `x-and-no-other` is pass 5 of 25 in the pipeline. It changes 22 of the 1776 formulas of the sweep.

The shortest of them, as written in Alloy:

```text
all c: Cleanup, s: String | c.tags = "a"
```

Without the pass:

```text
For every cleanup, every text T1 and every text T2:
  the cleanup is tagged text T2 exactly when text T2 and "a" are the same.
```

With it:

```text
For every cleanup and every text:
  the cleanup is tagged "a" and is tagged no other text.
```

- Readers: A strict judge (Opus) found 46 of 46 changed statements lossless; two haiku readers got 16 of 16 situations right, "no other" over an empty set among them.
- Rejected: "no other" inside a noun phrase, as in "an owner that no other owner is the parent of": it covers less than the claim.
- Rejected: a field of at most one value: its reading already says it, "owner_1 is the home of the cleanup".
<!-- pass-x-and-no-other:end -->

#### @spec two-values-that-are-equal-are-said-member-by-member

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `y.f = z.g` as "for every" member of the type of `f`, the reading of `f` "exactly when" the reading of `g`. When one side is primed, it says that side "at the next moment" and the other "now". It says `y.f != z.g` as the negation of that.

This follows because two sets are equal exactly when they have the same members. The type of the field holds every member that either side can have.

#### @spec an-expression-is-said-through-the-types-of-its-columns

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says a [*formula*](#term-formula) about an expression through members of the types of its columns. This holds for an expression that is more than a set or a navigation of a variable.

This follows because the vocabulary declares the types of what an expression can hold. A claim about what it holds is then a claim about each member of those types, which the readings say.

##### @spec a-union-on-the-right-is-said-as-or

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `x in a + b`, for a variable or a pair `x`, as `x in a` or `x in b`.

This follows because a member of a union is a member of one of its parts.

##### @spec an-intersection-on-the-right-is-said-as-and

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `x in a & b`, for a variable or a pair `x`, as `x in a` and `x in b`.

This follows because a member of an intersection is a member of both of its parts.

##### @spec not-in-before-a-difference-is-said-as-the-negation-of-in

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `x not in a - b` as the negation of `x in a - b`: `x not in a` or `x in b`.

This follows because `not in` is the negation of `in`.

##### @spec membership-in-a-navigation-of-an-expression-is-said-as-a-pair-in-it

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `x in y.e`, for a variable `y`, as `y->x in e`, and `x in e.y` as `x->y in e`.

This follows because `y` is one thing, so `y.e` holds what `e` pairs with `y`.

##### @spec a-pair-in-a-product-is-said-as-each-side-in-its-part

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `x->y in a -> b` as `x in a` and `y in b`.

This follows because a product holds every pair of a member of `a` and a member of `b`, and nothing else.

##### @spec membership-in-a-chain-of-navigations-is-said-through-a-member-between

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `x in e.f`, where `e` is not one variable, as `some m: T | m in e and x in m.f`. `T` is the type of the last column of `e`.

This follows because `e.f` holds what `f` gives a member of `e`, and every member of `e` is a member of `T`.

##### @spec membership-in-a-navigation-from-a-signature-is-said-through-a-member-of-it

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `x in S.f`, for a signature `S` where `S.f` has no reading of its own, as `some m: S | m->x in f`: "a cleanup is on x".

This follows because `S.f` holds what `f` gives some member of `S`.

##### @spec membership-in-a-signature-with-no-reading-is-said-with-its-noun

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `x in S`, for a signature `S` with a noun and no reading, as `x` "is" the noun with its article: "c is a cleanup".

This follows because to be in a signature is to be one of its kind, which its noun names.

##### @spec a-primed-expression-is-said-at-the-next-moment

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `x in e'`, for an expression `e`, as "at the next moment" before `x in e`.

This follows because a variable is the same thing at every moment, so the prime moves only `e`.

##### @spec an-expression-of-a-variable-on-the-left-is-said-member-by-member

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `e in s`, for an expression `e` that names a variable, as: for every member `m` of the type of `e`, when `m in e`, `m in s`.

This follows because one set is in another exactly when each of its members is.

##### @spec two-expressions-that-are-equal-are-said-member-by-member

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `a = b`, for sides that the specs above do not say, as: for every member `m` of their type, `m in a` exactly when `m in b`. It says `a != b` as the negation of that.

This follows because two sets are equal exactly when they have the same members.

##### @spec some-or-no-of-an-expression-is-said-over-the-types-of-its-columns

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `some e` and `no e`, for an expression the specs above do not say, as `some` or `no` over its column types, with the members in `e`.

This follows because an expression holds something exactly when some members of its types are in it.

##### @spec one-or-lone-of-an-expression-is-said-as-exactly-or-at-most-one

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `one e` and `lone e` as exactly one or at most one member of the types of the columns of `e` in `e`.

This follows because `one e` holds when `e` holds one member, and `lone e` when it holds at most one.

##### @spec an-expression-whose-types-the-vocabulary-does-not-tell-is-refused

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses a [*formula*](#term-formula) about an expression whose column types the vocabulary does not tell, and names the expression.

This follows because a member of a type the verbalizer guessed could leave out what the expression holds.

#### @spec an-override-is-said-as-the-pairs-of-its-right-and-the-rest-of-its-left

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `x->y in r ++ s` as `x->y in s`, or `x->y in r` and `no x.s`. For sets, `x in a ++ b` is `x in a + b`.

Derives from: [`spec-an-expression-is-said-through-the-types-of-its-columns`](#spec-an-expression-is-said-through-the-types-of-its-columns)

This follows because an override keeps the pairs of `s` and the pairs of `r` whose first member `s` relates to nothing. A set relates nothing, so its override is its union.

#### @spec a-domain-restriction-is-said-as-the-first-member-in-the-set

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `x->y in a <: r` as `x in a` and `x->y in r`.

Derives from: [`spec-an-expression-is-said-through-the-types-of-its-columns`](#spec-an-expression-is-said-through-the-types-of-its-columns)

This follows because `a <: r` keeps the pairs of `r` whose first member is in `a`.

#### @spec a-range-restriction-is-said-as-the-last-member-in-the-set

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `x->y in r :> b` as `x->y in r` and `y in b`.

Derives from: [`spec-an-expression-is-said-through-the-types-of-its-columns`](#spec-an-expression-is-said-through-the-types-of-its-columns)

This follows because `r :> b` keeps the pairs of `r` whose last member is in `b`.

#### @spec an-arrow-with-a-multiplicity-is-refused

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses an arrow with a multiplicity, such as `a one -> lone b`, and says that it says how many each side relates.

This follows because a multiplicity on an arrow says how many things a relation pairs with each member, and no reading says that.

#### @spec a-closure-is-said-as-reaching-in-one-or-more-steps

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `x->y in ^r` as `x` "reaches" `y` "in one or more steps", and says what a step is with the reading of `r`.

Derives from: [`spec-an-expression-is-said-through-the-types-of-its-columns`](#spec-an-expression-is-said-through-the-types-of-its-columns)

This follows because `^r` holds `x->y` exactly when a chain of pairs of `r` leads from `x` to `y`.

#### @spec a-reflexive-closure-is-said-as-reaching-in-zero-or-more-steps

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `x->y in *r` as `x` "reaches" `y` "in zero or more steps", and says what a step is with the reading of `r`.

Derives from: [`spec-a-closure-is-said-as-reaching-in-one-or-more-steps`](#spec-a-closure-is-said-as-reaching-in-one-or-more-steps)

This follows because `*r` is `^r` with every member paired with itself, which a chain of no steps reaches.

#### @spec some-or-no-of-a-reflexive-closure-is-refused

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses `some`, `no`, `one` or `lone` of a reflexive closure, and says that it holds every member of every type.

This follows because `*r` pairs every atom with itself, Int atoms included, and no type the vocabulary declares holds them all.

#### @spec none-is-said-as-nothing

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `e = none`, `none = e` and `e in none` as `no e`, and `e != none` as `some e`. It leaves `none` out of a union or a difference, and says `x in none` alone as never holding. It takes `none in e`, and a [*quantifier*](#term-quantifier) over `none` but `some` and `one`, as always holding, and says `#none` as 0.

This follows because `none` holds nothing.

#### @spec a-quantifier-over-a-variable-is-said-of-the-variable

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `all x: p | f` and `some x: p | f`, for a variable `p`, as `f` with `p` in the place of `x`, and `no x: p | f` as its negation.

This follows because a variable holds one thing, so a quantifier over it ranges over that thing alone. `lone x: p | f` always holds.

#### @spec a-value-in-its-own-builtin-type-always-holds

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) takes a string in `String`, and an integer variable in `Int`, as a [*formula*](#term-formula) that always holds.

This follows because a value is always in its own type. Alone such a formula claims nothing, and in an `and` it changes nothing.

#### @spec a-formula-that-never-holds-is-refused

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses a [*formula*](#term-formula) that never holds, such as `some none`, and says that it claims what cannot be.

This follows because no words of the readings say a formula that is always false, and words that seemed to would hide it.

#### @spec a-formula-that-never-holds-is-left-out-of-an-or

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) leaves a [*formula*](#term-formula) that never holds, such as `x in none`, out of an `or`.

This follows because `a or false` claims what `a` claims.

#### @spec a-pair-in-iden-is-said-as-the-same

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `x->y in iden` as `x` and `y` being the same.

This follows because `iden` pairs each atom with itself, and nothing else.

#### @spec univ-is-said-as-a-signature-of-its-own

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `univ` as a signature that holds every atom, with the noun the readings give it.

This follows because `univ` is the set of every atom, a signature that no declaration names. Without a noun of its own, a quantifier over it is refused as any type with no noun is.

#### @spec a-set-comprehension-is-said-through-its-variables

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `x in { y: T | f }` as `x in T` and `f` with `x` in the place of `y`, and `{ y: T }` as `T`.

Derives from: [`spec-an-expression-is-said-through-the-types-of-its-columns`](#spec-an-expression-is-said-through-the-types-of-its-columns)

This follows because the comprehension holds the members of `T` for which `f` holds.

#### @spec disj-of-expressions-is-said-as-no-two-sharing-a-member

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `disj[a, b]` as `a` and `b` being different when both are variables, and as `no a & b` otherwise. Over more arguments, it says it of each pair.

This follows because `disj` holds when no two of its arguments share a member.

#### @spec a-string-is-said-as-itself-in-quotes

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says a string in the place of a variable as itself, in quotes: "c is named "abc"".

This follows because a string is one thing, and its quotes show the reader where it starts and ends.

#### @spec an-expression-is-one-thing-where-its-declarations-make-it-so

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) takes an expression for one thing only where the declarations make it so. That covers a variable, a string and a number. It also covers a navigation of a `one` field from one thing, and such an expression primed.

This follows because a rewrite that takes an expression for one thing is lossless only when it holds exactly one. The kind of syntax does not tell that: `c.name` is one thing when `name` is a `one` field, and `c.tags` is not when `tags` is a `set` field.

#### @spec a-variable-a-quantifier-declares-has-the-type-it-declares

> In the types of the columns of an expression, the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) takes a variable to be of the type its [*quantifier*](#term-quantifier) declares.

This follows because an expression such as `on ++ (c -> o)` has the types of `on` only if `c` and `o` have them too. Without them, the verbalizer would refuse an override that updates a state.

#### @spec a-variable-on-the-right-of-in-is-said-as-equal-to-what-is-in-it

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `x in p`, for a variable `p` that a [*quantifier*](#term-quantifier) declares, as `x = p` where `x` is one thing. Where `x` can hold several things, it says that each of them is `p`.

This follows because a variable holds one thing, so what is in it is that thing. A name that no quantifier declares is not known to hold one thing, and is still refused when it has no reading.

#### @spec some-or-no-of-a-signature-is-said-over-its-members

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `some S`, `no S`, `one S` and `lone S` of a signature `S` with a noun and no reading by its noun alone, as `there is an owner`.

This follows because `some S` claims that `S` has a member, and the noun of `S` names one. The words need no variable.

#### @spec a-count-of-one-thing-is-a-formula-that-always-or-never-holds

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) takes `some`, `one` and `lone` of one thing as a [*formula*](#term-formula) that always holds, and `no` of one thing as one that never does.

This follows because one thing is exactly one. The verbalizer leaves such a formula out of an `and` or an `or` where it changes nothing. Alone, it refuses it, as it refuses the other formulas that always or never hold.

#### @spec a-value-in-a-string-is-said-as-equal-to-it

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `x in "a"`, where `x` is [one thing](#spec-an-expression-is-one-thing-where-its-declarations-make-it-so), as `x = "a"`: "c and "a" are the same". It says `x not in "a"` as `x != "a"`.

Derives from: [`spec-a-string-is-said-as-itself-in-quotes`](#spec-a-string-is-said-as-itself-in-quotes)

This follows because `x` is one thing and a string is one thing, so `x` is in the string exactly when the two are the same. A left side that can hold none or several things is not one thing: `c.tags in "a"` holds when `c.tags` is empty, and `c.tags = "a"` does not. The verbalizer says such a side member by member, as [`spec-an-expression-of-a-variable-on-the-left-is-said-member-by-member`](#spec-an-expression-of-a-variable-on-the-left-is-said-member-by-member) says.

#### @spec set-or-seq-before-an-expression-is-refused

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses `set e` and `seq e` as a [*formula*](#term-formula), and says that Alloy reads them only in a declaration.

This follows because the analyzer does not read either as a formula, so neither claims anything.

#### @spec a-rule-of-two-clauses-is-said-on-one-line

<!-- statement-spec-a-rule-of-two-clauses-is-said-on-one-line:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> When all of these hold:
> - a [*list*](#term-series) is a rule whose two sides are each one clause
> - the list is not a rule whose first side begins with a time phrase
>
> then the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says the list on one line, as "when" the first side, the second side.
<!-- statement-spec-a-rule-of-two-clauses-is-said-on-one-line:end -->

A short rule reads best as one sentence. Laid out with a line per side, `all c: Cleanup | c in Ran implies c in Registered` breaks before `then code has registered the cleanup`. On one line it reads `When a cleanup has run, code has registered the cleanup`. A first side that opens with a time phrase stays off one line. In `when at the next moment, c has run, d has run`, the phrase seems to cover d too.

<details>
<summary>Alloy</summary>

```alloy
all f: Series | (f in OneLineRule and f not in TimeFirst) implies f in OneLine
```

</details>

<!-- pass-rule-on-one-line:begin — generated by `node test/core/wordings.ts --write`; edits are overwritten -->
The pass `rule-on-one-line` is pass 20 of 25 in the pipeline. It changes 274 of the 1776 formulas of the sweep.

The shortest of them, as written in Alloy:

```text
all c: Cleanup | c in Ran implies c in Registered
```

Without the pass:

```text
When a cleanup has run
then code has registered the cleanup.
```

With it:

```text
When a cleanup has run, code has registered the cleanup.
```
<!-- pass-rule-on-one-line:end -->

#### @spec two-rules-that-go-each-way-are-said-as-one-equivalence

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says two rules as one equivalence of their sides where three things hold. Both stand in one list of claims that hold together. Neither has an "otherwise". The first side of each is the second side of the other. Where one side is a run of clauses joined by "and" or "or", it is the second side of the equivalence.

This follows because a rule each way is what `iff` claims. Two rules say each side twice, and the reader has to compare them to see that they go both ways. "Exactly when" says it once.

The run of clauses goes second, so that the claim of one clause leads. "The checker writes the statement" comes first, and "the statement is unwritten or stale" after it.

<!-- pass-rules-as-equivalence:begin — generated by `node test/core/wordings.ts --write`; edits are overwritten -->
The pass `rules-as-equivalence` is pass 3 of 25 in the pipeline. It changes 2 of the 1776 formulas of the sweep.

The shortest of them, as written in Alloy:

```text
all c: Cleanup | (c in Ran implies c in Registered) and (c in Registered implies c in Ran)
```

Without the pass:

```text
For every cleanup:
  all of these hold:
    - when the cleanup has run, code has registered the cleanup
    - when code has registered the cleanup, the cleanup has run
```

With it:

```text
For every cleanup:
  code has registered the cleanup exactly when the cleanup has run.
```
<!-- pass-rules-as-equivalence:end -->

#### @spec an-equivalence-of-two-clauses-is-said-with-exactly-when

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `a iff b`, when each side is one clause, as `a` "exactly when" `b`.

This follows because "exactly when" says that each side holds when the other does, which is what `iff` claims.

<!-- pass-exactly-when:begin — generated by `node test/core/wordings.ts --write`; edits are overwritten -->
The pass `exactly-when` is pass 19 of 25 in the pipeline. It changes 41 of the 1776 formulas of the sweep.

The shortest of them, as written in Alloy:

```text
all c: Cleanup | (c in Ran implies c in Registered) and (c in Registered implies c in Ran)
```

Without the pass:

```text
For every cleanup:
  both or neither of these hold:
    - code has registered the cleanup
    - the cleanup has run
```

With it:

```text
For every cleanup:
  code has registered the cleanup exactly when the cleanup has run.
```
<!-- pass-exactly-when:end -->

#### @spec an-equivalence-of-more-than-clauses-is-said-as-both-or-neither

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `a iff b`, when a side is more than one clause, as a [*list*](#term-series) of the two sides under "both or neither of these hold".

This follows because "exactly when" between two lists or rules would not show where each side ends.

#### @spec an-equivalence-that-is-a-side-of-a-rule-is-said-as-both-or-neither

> As a side of a rule, of a binary temporal operator or of a [*definition*](#term-definition-passage), the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `a iff b` as both or neither.

This follows because "exactly when" inside "when …, …", or after the "exactly when" of a definition, could take the whole sentence as its side.

#### @spec an-equivalence-whose-first-side-begins-with-a-time-phrase-is-said-as-both-or-neither

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `a iff b` as both or neither of its sides when `a` begins with a time phrase. A clause at the next moment and a clause now are the exception.

This follows because the time phrase at the start would read as covering both sides, where the formula has it cover `a`.

#### @spec a-clause-at-the-next-moment-equal-to-a-clause-now-is-said-with-exactly-when

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `a' iff b`, for clauses with no other time phrase, comma, "and", "or" or relative clause, as `a` "at the next moment exactly when" `b` "now".

This follows because the time phrase then ends its own clause, and "now" marks the other. Neither can reach across "exactly when". A frame condition such as `Ran' = Ran` reads this way, member by member.

#### @spec an-equivalence-whose-first-side-holds-a-noun-phrase-is-said-as-both-or-neither

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `a iff b` as both or neither of its sides when `a` holds a noun phrase, such as "no owner".

This follows because "exactly when" follows `a` with no comma between. A reader could take it as part of the noun phrase, "no owner exactly when …", where the formula has it join the two sides.

#### @spec an-else-is-said-as-otherwise

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `c implies a else b` as the rule "when" `c`, `a`, with "otherwise" before `b`.

This follows because `b` is claimed exactly when `c` does not hold, which is what "otherwise" says.

#### @spec a-sentence-starts-with-a-capital-only-where-it-starts-with-its-own-words

> A statement begins with a capital where it begins with its own words, and with the name unchanged where it begins with a name.

This follows because a name from the formula, such as a variable, stays as it is.

#### @spec two-variables-are-said-to-be-different-or-the-same

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says a comparison of two variables as "different" or "the same".

This follows because the logic compares two things, and the reader should hear that they are two, or one.

#### @spec eventually-is-said-as-now-or-later

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `eventually` as "now or later".

This follows because eventually includes the present moment, and "someday" or "sooner or later" would leave it out. "Now or later" names both, in the words people use.

#### @spec after-is-said-as-at-the-next-moment

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `after` as "at the next moment".

This follows because after looks one step ahead and no further.

#### @spec always-is-said-as-from-now-on

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `always` as "from now on", unless what it covers is a rule.

This follows because always holds from the present on, the present included. "At every moment" would also reach back to the moments before it, which historically covers.

#### @spec a-rule-at-every-later-moment-is-said-from-now-on-whenever

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `always` over a rule as "from now on, whenever" the rule's condition, followed by its consequence.

This follows because a rule that holds at every moment is what "whenever" means in plain English. "From now on" keeps the start at the present, as `always` alone does. So the words still leave the moments before it out.

- Readers: Two passes of a strict judge (Opus) found 98 of 102 sampled statements lossless; the 4 failures came from the old "a moment before", now "a moment just before".
- Readers: On a canon of 41 rules, a judge rated 25 as reading as well as the handwritten claim, against none before.
- Rejected: "whenever" over a rule that says "now" or a moment before: its "now" would count from each moment "whenever" picks.
