#### @spec before-is-said-as-there-is-a-moment-just-before-and-at-it

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `before` as `there is a moment just before, and at it`.

This follows because before looks one step back, and fails at the first moment, which has no moment before it. "At the moment before" would leave that out, and "a moment before" alone would read as any earlier moment, which once covers.

#### @spec once-is-said-as-now-or-earlier

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `once` as "now or earlier".

This follows because once is eventually turned to the past, and includes the present moment as eventually does.

#### @spec historically-is-said-as-now-and-at-every-earlier-moment

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `historically` as "now and at every earlier moment".

This follows because historically is always turned to the past, and includes the present moment as always does.

#### @spec a-sequence-is-said-as-and-at-the-next-moment

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `a ; b` as "a, and at the next moment, b".

This follows because the semicolon says that the first side holds now and the second side holds at the next moment.

#### @spec a-time-phrase-before-words-that-hold-a-time-phrase-sets-them-apart

> Before words with a time phrase of their own, the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) ends a time phrase with a colon and sets the words apart below it.

This follows because two time phrases in a row, such as "from now on, at the next moment", read as one moment. A reader could also take a second "at the next moment" later in the words as the moment of the first.

<!-- pass-time-phrase-in-front:begin — generated by `node test/core/wordings.ts --write`; edits are overwritten -->
The pass `time-phrase-in-front` is pass 16 of 25 in the pipeline. It changes 341 of the 1776 formulas of the sweep.

The shortest of them, as written in Alloy:

```text
always all c: Cleanup | c in Ran
```

Without the pass:

```text
From now on:
  for every cleanup:
    the cleanup has run.
```

With it:

```text
From now on, for every cleanup:
  the cleanup has run.
```
<!-- pass-time-phrase-in-front:end -->

#### @spec an-and-or-an-or-below-a-time-phrase-is-a-list

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says an "and" or an "or" that a time phrase covers as a [*list*](#term-series) below it, and never as one sentence after it.

This follows because in "at the next moment, a or b" a reader can take the time phrase as covering `a` alone, with `b` read as now. As a heading over a list, the phrase covers every item.

#### @spec the-spellings-of-not-in-and-not-equal-are-said-alike

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `!in`, `! in`, `not =` and `! =` as it says `not in` and `!=`.

This follows because Alloy reads each spelling as the same comparison.

#### @spec text-that-alloy-does-not-read-is-refused

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses a [*formula*](#term-formula) that Alloy does not read, such as `a == b`, with the reason the parser gives.

This follows because a formula the analyzer cannot read claims nothing, so no words can say it.

#### @spec a-binary-temporal-operator-is-said-with-its-sides-set-apart

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) sets each side of `until`, `since`, `releases` and `triggered` apart when either side is more than one plain clause, and each side of `;` that is. It puts them below the words that place them in time.

This follows because each operator bounds a stretch of moments by a moment where a side holds. On one line, the words name that moment as "the first moment where" or "the last moment where". A reader can count such a moment from the start of the run, or past now. Set apart, the moment is "the first such moment" after one counted from now, and the stretch says where it starts and ends. A longer side set apart also shows where it ends.

##### @spec until-is-said-as-two-parts

> When a side is more than one plain clause, the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `a until b` in two parts. First comes `b` "now or later", then `a` "at every moment from now until the first such moment, not including it".

This follows because until claims that `b` comes, now or later, and that `a` holds at every moment before it first does.

##### @spec since-is-said-as-two-parts

> When a side is more than one plain clause, the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `a since b` in two parts. First comes `b` "now or earlier", then `a` "at every moment after the last such moment, up to and including now".

This follows because since is until turned to the past.

##### @spec until-of-two-plain-clauses-is-one-sentence

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `a until b` of two plain clauses as one sentence: `b` "now or later, and until then," `a`.

This follows because a plain clause holds no time phrase, comma or relative clause. So "now or later" can only cover `b`, and "then" can only be a moment of `b` counted from now. "Until then" stops before that moment, as until does, and readers of every size took it that way.

<!-- pass-until-in-a-sentence:begin — generated by `node test/core/wordings.ts --write`; edits are overwritten -->
The pass `until-in-a-sentence` is pass 15 of 25 in the pipeline. It changes 40 of the 1776 formulas of the sweep.

The shortest of them, as written in Alloy:

```text
all c: Cleanup, o, p: Owner | (c in Ran until o in Disposed)
```

Without the pass:

```text
For every cleanup, every owner O1 and every owner O2:
  all of these hold:
    - now or later, the following holds:
        pulse has disposed owner O1
    - at every moment from now until the first such moment, not including it, the following holds:
        the cleanup has run.
```

With it:

```text
For every cleanup, every owner O1 and every owner O2:
  pulse has disposed owner O1 now or later, and until then, the cleanup has run.
```

- Readers: On 8 timelines built to catch each misreading, 5 of 5 readers (Opus, Sonnet, three haiku) read "until then" right; "first" is not needed, since any moment of b gives the same truth.
- Rejected: "up to the first such moment, but not necessarily at it": lossless, and longer than it needs to be.
- Rejected: "ever since", "since then" and "after that" for since: each misread by a haiku reader, as counting the moment of b itself or as its first moment; since needs the last.
<!-- pass-until-in-a-sentence:end -->

##### @spec since-of-two-plain-clauses-is-one-sentence

> Of two plain clauses, the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `a since b` as one sentence. It says `b` "now or earlier", then `a` "at every moment after the last such moment, up to and including now".

This follows because since is until turned to the past, and the same plain clauses leave its words one reading. "Ever since" would read as covering the moment of `b` too, so the words name the stretch in full.

##### @spec releases-is-said-as-always-or-until

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `a releases b` as `always b or (b until (a and b))`.

This follows because releases holds `b` up to and including the first moment where `a` holds, and for ever when that moment never comes. The two alternatives say each case.

##### @spec triggered-is-said-as-historically-or-since

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `a triggered b` as `historically b or (b since (a and b))`.

This follows because triggered is releases turned to the past.

##### @spec a-sequence-with-a-side-of-more-than-a-clause-is-said-as-and-at-the-next-moment

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `a ; b`, with a side that is more than one plain clause, as `a and after b`.

This follows because `a ; b` claims `a` now and `b` at the next moment, which `a and after b` claims too.

##### @spec a-side-with-a-time-phrase-a-noun-phrase-or-a-where-is-more-than-a-plain-clause

> A side is one plain clause only when the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says it by one reading with a variable in each of its places. It holds no time phrase, no comma, no noun phrase, no relative clause, no "where" and no "it is not the case that".

This follows because the words cannot mark the reach of any of these inline. After "c is on no owner", "now or later" could cover the whole side. It could also cover only "is on", which says that c is on no owner at every later moment. After "c has run or pulse has disposed o", it could cover only the last alternative.

#### @spec this-outside-a-definition-of-a-signature-is-refused

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses `this` outside a predicate or a function of a signature, which Alloy does not read.

This follows because the analyzer finds no name `this` there, so the formula claims nothing.

#### @spec steps-in-a-formula-is-refused

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses `steps` in a [*formula*](#term-formula), and says that Alloy reads it only in a scope.

This follows because the analyzer finds no name `steps` in a formula.

#### @spec a-name-of-this-module-is-said-as-the-name

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `this/Ran` and `@Ran` as it says `Ran`.

This follows because `this/` names the module the formula is in, and outside the fact of a signature, `@` changes nothing.

#### @spec a-name-of-another-module-is-said-by-its-own-reading

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says a name of another module, such as `m/Ran`, by the reading of that whole name.

This follows because two modules may each have a `Ran`, and the reading of one would not say the other.

#### @spec a-comment-in-a-formula-is-left-out

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) leaves out a comment in a [*formula*](#term-formula): `--`, `//`, `/* … */` and `/** … */`.

This follows because Alloy reads a comment as nothing, so it claims nothing.

#### @spec a-typographic-prime-is-said-as-a-prime

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `‘` and `’` as it says `'`.

This follows because Alloy reads all three as the prime.

#### @spec an-integer-comparison-is-said-in-integers-that-wrap

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `<`, `>`, `=<`, `>=` and their negations, and `=` and `!=` between two numbers, after "in integers that wrap around at the analyzer's bit width".

Derives from: [`fact-the-analyzer-wraps-integers-at-their-bit-width`](#fact-the-analyzer-wraps-integers-at-their-bit-width)

This follows because the words of arithmetic say what the analyzer computes only when the reader knows that its integers wrap around.

##### @spec two-numbers-are-compared-with-the-words-of-their-operator

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `<` as "is less than", `>` as "is greater than", `=<` as "is at most", `>=` as "is at least" and `=` as "is equal to". It says a negation with "not".

This follows because those words say the order of two numbers, and the words before them say the wrap once.

##### @spec a-count-is-said-as-the-number-of-values

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `#e` as "the number of values of" a member of the type of `e`, "such that" the member is in `e`.

This follows because `#e` counts the members of `e`.

##### @spec a-sum-over-a-variable-is-said-as-the-sum-over-every-value

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `sum x: T | e` as "the sum, over every" member of `T`, "of" `e`.

This follows because the sum adds the value of `e` for each member of `T`.

##### @spec a-set-of-integers-where-a-number-belongs-is-said-as-the-sum-of-its-members

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says a set of integers where a number belongs, as in `c.n < 3` or `int[c.n]`, as `"the sum of the values of"` an integer in it.

This follows because the analyzer reads a set of integers where a number belongs as the sum of its members, as `int` says.

##### @spec plus-minus-and-mul-are-said-as-plus-minus-and-times

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `plus[a, b]`, `minus[a, b]` and `mul[a, b]` as `a` "plus", "minus" or "times" `b`.

This follows because those are the words of the operations, and the comparison says that they wrap.

##### @spec a-division-is-said-with-its-rounding-and-its-rule-for-zero

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `div[a, b]` as `a` "divided by" `b`, rounded toward zero, with its value when `b` is zero. It says `rem[a, b]` as `"the remainder of"` `a` divided by `b`, with its sign and its value when `b` is zero.

Derives from: [`fact-the-analyzer-divides-toward-zero-and-gives-the-sign-for-zero`](#fact-the-analyzer-divides-toward-zero-and-gives-the-sign-for-zero)

This follows because the analyzer divides by zero, and rounds, in ways that ordinary words for division leave open.

##### @spec a-number-is-said-as-itself

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says a number in decimal, whether the [*formula*](#term-formula) writes it in decimal, in hexadecimal or in binary.

This follows because the value is what the formula claims, and the comparison says that it wraps.

##### @spec min-and-max-are-said-as-the-least-and-the-greatest-integer

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `min` and `max` as "the least integer" and "the greatest integer".

This follows because they are the ends of the range that the bit width gives.

##### @spec the-spellings-fun-min-fun-max-and-fun-next-are-said-as-min-max-and-next

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `fun/min`, `fun/max` and `fun/next` as it says `min`, `max` and `next`.

This follows because the analyzer reads each spelling as the same integer or relation. A spelling said as its name would leave the reader without its meaning.

##### @spec a-part-of-an-integer-comparison-that-is-more-than-a-number-is-named-below-it

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) names a count, a sum or a division in an integer comparison as `number_1`, `number_2` and so on, and says after "where" what each is.

This follows because the words of a count end in a clause of their own. Two of them in one sentence would read two ways.

##### @spec a-shift-is-refused

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses `<<`, `>>` and `>>>`, and says that the analyzer shifts by the lowest bits of the amount.

Derives from: [`fact-the-analyzer-shifts-by-the-lowest-bits-of-the-amount`](#fact-the-analyzer-shifts-by-the-lowest-bits-of-the-amount)

This follows because words for a shift by an amount the bits do not hold would have to count bits. Plain words would say a different shift.

##### @spec a-set-compared-with-a-number-is-refused

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses `=` and `!=` between a set and a number, such as `c.n = 2`, and names them.

This follows because Alloy reads them as sets, which compare the set with the one integer of the number. The words would have to say both the sets and the wrap of the number.

##### @spec a-number-outside-an-integer-comparison-is-refused

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses a number or a count outside an integer comparison, and names it.

This follows because outside a comparison, the number is an integer atom of the analyzer's range. No words there say that it wraps.

#### @spec the-next-integer-is-said-as-the-integer-after

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `x->y in next` as `y` "is the integer after" `x` "without wrapping around".

This follows because `next` pairs each integer with the one after it, and the greatest integer with none. Integer arithmetic wraps, and the words of a comparison say so. Without the last words, the integer after the greatest would read as the least.

#### @spec int-and-seq-int-have-nouns-of-their-own

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `Int` with the noun "integer", and `seq/Int` with the noun "sequence index", unless the readings give another.

This follows because Alloy declares both signatures, so no vocabulary gives them a noun.

#### @spec a-name-with-no-reading-is-refused-and-named

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses a [*formula*](#term-formula) with a name that has no reading, and names the word.

This follows because a statement that skips the name says less than the logic holds. The author can mend only what the verbalizer names.

#### @spec a-reading-with-no-negative-form-is-refused-and-named

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses a [*formula*](#term-formula) that negates a word whose reading has no negative form, and names the word.

This follows because the verbalizer would have to invent a negation, and the invention may mean something else.

#### @spec a-type-with-no-noun-is-refused-and-named

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses a [*formula*](#term-formula) that quantifies a type with no noun, and names the type.

This follows because a quantifier without a noun for its type cannot say what its variable stands for.

#### @spec a-reading-that-uses-a-slot-the-formula-does-not-give-is-refused

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses a [*formula*](#term-formula) whose reading of a word uses a place that the formula does not fill, and names the place.

This follows because the reading talks about something the formula does not mention, and any word put there would be invented.

#### @spec a-reading-that-leaves-out-a-slot-the-formula-gives-is-refused

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses a [*formula*](#term-formula) whose reading of a word leaves out a place that the formula fills, and names the place.

This follows because the variable in that place would drop out of the statement, which would then say less than the formula.

#### @spec a-binary-temporal-operator-inside-a-side-of-another-is-refused

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses `until`, `since`, `releases`, `triggered` or `;` with a side that holds one of them, except a `;` after a `;`.

This follows because the words of each one are a clause with commas, and two of them nested read in more than one way. A chain of `;` reads in order, each later step set apart below the "at the next moment" of the one before it.

#### @spec a-primed-relation-of-a-variable-signature-is-refused

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses a prime on a relation `Sig.rel` that has a reading of its own when `Sig` is a `var sig`.

This follows because the prime then moves the signature to the next moment too. "At the next moment" in front would say that, but the reading of the relation names the signature as it is now.

#### @spec a-construct-the-words-do-not-cover-is-refused

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses a [*formula*](#term-formula) with a construct that the words do not cover, and names the construct.

This follows because leaving a construct out would hide part of the logic, and guessing its words could change its meaning.

#### @spec a-line-of-readings-that-cannot-be-read-is-refused

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses a [*line*](#term-line) of readings that has neither a noun nor a key, and says that it cannot read the line.

This follows because a line the verbalizer misreads would give a word the wrong sentence.

#### @spec a-bracket-with-no-partner-is-refused

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses a [*line*](#term-line) of readings with a bracket that has no partner, and says so.

This follows because a bracket marks the word that links to a term, and half a mark would link the wrong words.

#### @spec a-predicate-whose-body-cannot-be-said-is-refused-with-advice-to-give-it-a-reading

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses a [*call*](#term-predicate-call) of a predicate with no reading and a body the words do not cover, and advises a reading.

This follows because a body the verbalizer cannot say is no fallback, and the reading is how the author mends it.

#### @spec a-predicate-defined-in-terms-of-itself-is-refused

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses a [*call*](#term-predicate-call) of a predicate whose body calls that predicate, and says that it calls itself.

This follows because a body that calls itself never ends in words.

#### @spec a-call-with-the-wrong-number-of-arguments-is-refused

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses a [*call*](#term-predicate-call) with the wrong number of arguments, and says how many the predicate takes.

This follows because an argument with no parameter, or a parameter with no argument, has no place in the words.

#### @spec text-that-is-not-a-definition-is-refused

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses text given as a [*definition*](#term-definition-passage) that is not one, and says how to write a definition.

This follows because the verbalizer words a definition as one, and text that only looks like a formula would get the wrong words.

#### @spec a-parameter-with-no-type-is-refused

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses a [*definition*](#term-definition-passage) with a parameter that has no type, and says so.

This follows because the statement says "for every" a noun of the type, and a parameter without a type has no noun.

#### @spec a-definition-whose-body-is-a-rule-is-said-with-the-rule-set-apart

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says a [*definition*](#term-definition-passage) whose body is a rule or a "for every" as what it names "exactly when the following holds". It sets the body apart below.

This follows because "exactly when" before a rule on the same line would leave the reader to guess where the body ends.

#### @spec a-definition-of-a-word-with-no-reading-is-refused

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses a [*definition*](#term-definition-passage) of a word that has no reading, and names the word.

This follows because the statement of a definition says the word it defines, and without a reading it would say nothing.

#### @spec a-passage-that-starts-with-pred-is-a-definition

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) reads text that starts with the keyword `pred` as a [*definition*](#term-definition-passage).

This follows because the keyword is how the author says that the text defines a word.

#### @spec a-passage-that-starts-with-fun-is-a-definition

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) reads text that starts with the keyword `fun` as a [*definition*](#term-definition-passage).

Derives from: [`spec-a-passage-that-starts-with-pred-is-a-definition`](#spec-a-passage-that-starts-with-pred-is-a-definition)

This follows because a function defines a word too: the name of its value.

#### @spec private-before-a-definition-changes-nothing-that-is-said

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says a `private pred` or a `private fun` as it says the same [*definition*](#term-definition-passage) without `private`.

This follows because `private` says where Alloy lets the name be used, and nothing about what it means.

#### @spec parameters-in-round-brackets-are-read-as-in-square-ones

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) reads `pred p(x: T)` as `pred p[x: T]`.

This follows because Alloy reads both brackets alike.

#### @spec a-comma-before-or-after-the-parameters-is-read-as-none

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) reads `pred p[, x: T]` and `pred p[x: T,]` as `pred p[x: T]`.

This follows because Alloy reads a comma at either end of the list as nothing.

#### @spec a-predicate-of-a-signature-takes-this-as-its-first-parameter

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) reads `pred T.p[x: U] { … }` as `pred p[this: T, x: U] { … }`, for its [*definition*](#term-definition-passage) and for a [*call*](#term-predicate-call) of it.

This follows because Alloy reads a predicate of a signature as one whose first parameter is `this`, of that signature.

#### @spec a-body-of-several-formulas-is-said-as-them-holding-together

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says a block of formulas on lines of their own, as a body or as a [*formula*](#term-formula), as the formulas holding together.

This follows because Alloy reads the formulas of a block as joined by `and`.

#### @spec an-empty-body-is-said-as-what-the-definition-names

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says a [*definition*](#term-definition-passage) with an empty body as what it names, for every parameter.

This follows because an empty body always holds, so the predicate holds for every value of each parameter.

#### @spec a-formula-that-always-holds-is-left-out-of-an-and

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) leaves a [*formula*](#term-formula) that always holds out of an `and`. An empty block is one, and so is a [*call*](#term-predicate-call) of a predicate with an empty body.

This follows because `a and true` claims what `a` claims.

#### @spec a-formula-that-only-always-holds-is-refused

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses a [*formula*](#term-formula) that always holds and is not part of an `and`, and says that it claims nothing.

This follows because no words of the readings say a formula that claims nothing, and a statement that said nothing would hide that.

#### @spec a-parameter-that-can-hold-several-things-or-none-is-refused

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses a [*definition*](#term-definition-passage) with a parameter declared with `lone`, `some` or `set`, or with an arrow, and names the parameter.

Derives from: [`spec-a-variable-that-can-hold-several-things-or-none-is-refused`](#spec-a-variable-that-can-hold-several-things-or-none-is-refused)

This follows because the definition says "for every" value of each parameter, and the readings have no words for every set of things.

#### @spec a-function-is-said-as-its-value-holding-a-member-exactly-when-its-body-does

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `fun f[x: T]: U { e }` as: for every `x` and every member `u` of `U`, the reading of `f` of `x` and `u` "exactly when" `u in e`.

This follows because a function names its value, and its value holds a member exactly when the body does.

#### @spec a-call-of-a-function-with-a-reading-is-said-with-its-reading

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says `y in f[x]`, for a function `f` with a reading, with the reading of `f`, with `x` and then `y` in its slots.

This follows because the reading says when the value of `f` holds a member, which is what `y in f[x]` claims.

#### @spec a-call-of-a-function-with-no-reading-is-said-by-its-body

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says a [*call*](#term-predicate-call) of a function with no reading by its body, with each argument in the place of its parameter.

Derives from: [`spec-a-predicate-with-no-reading-is-said-by-its-body`](#spec-a-predicate-with-no-reading-is-said-by-its-body)

This follows because the value of a call is the body with the arguments in place.

#### @spec a-call-of-a-macro-is-said-by-its-body

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says a [*call*](#term-predicate-call) of a macro, `let m[x] = …` or `let m[x] { … }`, by its body with each argument in the place of its parameter.

This follows because Alloy puts a macro's body in the place of each call, with an argument for each parameter.

#### @spec a-macro-as-a-definition-is-refused

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses a macro given as a [*definition*](#term-definition-passage), and says that a parameter of a macro has no type.

Derives from: [`spec-a-parameter-with-no-type-is-refused`](#spec-a-parameter-with-no-type-is-refused)

This follows because the verbalizer says a definition "for every" value of each parameter, and a parameter with no type has no noun.

#### @spec a-definition-says-what-it-names-exactly-when-its-body-holds-for-every-parameter

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says a [*definition*](#term-definition-passage) as "for every" parameter, then the name, "exactly when", and the body.

This follows because a definition fixes the meaning of a word for every value, and "exactly when" says that it holds in both directions.

#### @spec a-definition-that-marks-its-variables-disj-is-said-with-them-different

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says a [*definition*](#term-definition-passage) that marks its variables `disj` with the condition that they are different. A [*call*](#term-predicate-call) of it said by its body gets the same condition.

This follows because `disj` before the variables of a predicate adds that condition to its body.

#### @spec a-definition-with-a-body-of-one-clause-is-said-on-one-line

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says a [*definition*](#term-definition-passage) whose body is one clause on one line after the "for every".

This follows because a short definition is clearest as one sentence.

#### @spec a-definition-whose-body-is-a-series-sets-it-apart

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) sets apart the body of a [*definition*](#term-definition-passage) that is a [*series*](#term-series), below "exactly when the following holds".

This follows because a series after "exactly when" could end before its last clause and leave that clause outside the definition. "x is quiet exactly when x has run, and at the next moment, x has stopped" reads two ways. The verbalizer sets apart a side of a rule that holds a series for the same reason. The sweep found three such definitions once its reading back took in definitions too.

#### @spec a-definition-says-each-parameter-with-the-noun-of-its-type

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says each parameter of a [*definition*](#term-definition-passage) with the noun of its type.

This follows because each parameter is a thing, and the noun tells which kind.

#### @spec a-line-that-opens-a-part-ends-in-a-line-break-in-markdown

> In the Markdown layout, a line that opens a part of the statement ends in a line break, `\`, when a line of text follows. A blank line stays only after a [*list*](#term-series), where a line break cannot end the list.

This follows because a line break keeps the part on a line of its own with no empty line above it. The statement then takes the fewest lines that show its parts. Text right after a list would read as part of its last item, so a blank line ends the list.

#### @spec a-definition-is-said-in-markdown-the-way-a-formula-is

> In the Markdown layout, the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says a [*definition*](#term-definition-passage) in the lines it says a [*formula*](#term-formula) in.

This follows because the statement sits in a Markdown document, and a definition in it reads as paragraphs like any other statement.

#### @spec a-definition-by-cases-is-said-as-a-noun-phrase-for-each-kind

<!-- statement-spec-a-definition-by-cases-is-said-as-a-noun-phrase-for-each-kind:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> When all of these hold:
> - the alternatives of a [*definition*](#term-definition-passage) each begin with the kind of the subject
> - the definition can be said [*kind by kind*](#term-by-kind)
>
> then the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says the definition as a list with a noun phrase for each kind, such as "a spec that cites no axiom".
<!-- statement-spec-a-definition-by-cases-is-said-as-a-noun-phrase-for-each-kind:end -->

As it stands, a definition by cases repeats its subject in every case: `unit U1 is a spec`, `unit U1 cites no unit that is an axiom`, nested under `all of these hold`. The verbalizer instead names each kind once, as the head of a noun phrase: `a spec that cites no axiom and cites no spec`. The list then has one line per kind, and the reader sees at once what each kind must do. This applies when the verbalizer can say the definition [*kind by kind*](#term-by-kind).

<details>
<summary>Alloy</summary>

```alloy
all f: Definition | (f in GuardedByKind and byKind[f]) implies f in PhrasePerKind
```

</details>

<!-- pass-definition-by-kinds:begin — generated by `node test/core/wordings.ts --write`; edits are overwritten -->
The pass `definition-by-kinds` is pass 13 of 25 in the pipeline. It changes 2 of the 1776 formulas of the sweep.

The shortest of them, as written in Alloy:

```text
pred kept[x: univ] { x in Cleanup and x in Ran }
```

Without the pass:

```text
A thing is kept exactly when the thing is a cleanup and has run.
```

With it:

```text
A thing is kept exactly when the thing is a cleanup that has run.
```
<!-- pass-definition-by-kinds:end -->

#### @spec the-alternatives-of-one-kind-are-put-together-with-or

<!-- statement-spec-the-alternatives-of-one-kind-are-put-together-with-or:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> When a [*definition*](#term-definition-passage) has two alternatives for one kind and can be said [*kind by kind*](#term-by-kind), the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says the definition as one noun phrase for that kind, with the alternatives joined by or.
<!-- statement-spec-the-alternatives-of-one-kind-are-put-together-with-or:end -->

A canon often gives one kind two cases, as term-unfounded does: an exception without a spec, and an exception without a fact. Listed apart, two lines would begin "an exception that", as if the kind came twice. The verbalizer merges them into one phrase joined by "or": `an exception that cites no spec or cites no fact`. Each kind then keeps exactly one line in the list.

<details>
<summary>Alloy</summary>

```alloy
all f: Definition | (f in SameKindTwice and byKind[f]) implies f in JoinedWithOr
```

</details>

#### @spec the-options-of-an-or-inside-a-kind-are-one-coordination

<!-- statement-spec-the-options-of-an-or-inside-a-kind-are-one-coordination:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> When a [*definition*](#term-definition-passage) has an or inside one kind and can be said [*kind by kind*](#term-by-kind), the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says the definition as one run of clauses joined by commas and or.
<!-- statement-spec-the-options-of-an-or-inside-a-kind-are-one-coordination:end -->

A kind can hold its own choice, as in `a bug, and it names no issue or names an unknown issue or is not tested`. Said as it stands, that choice nests a second `at least one of these holds` under the kind. The verbalizer flattens it into one run after "that": `a bug that names no issue, names an issue that tracker does not know or is not tested`. Commas and a single "or" carry the run, so it reads in one pass.

<details>
<summary>Alloy</summary>

```alloy
all f: Definition | (f in OrInsideKind and byKind[f]) implies f in OneCoordination
```

</details>

#### @spec a-definition-with-one-kind-is-one-sentence

<!-- statement-spec-a-definition-with-one-kind-is-one-sentence:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> When the alternatives of a [*definition*](#term-definition-passage) are of one kind and the definition can be said [*kind by kind*](#term-by-kind), the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says the definition as one sentence.
<!-- statement-spec-a-definition-with-one-kind-is-one-sentence:end -->

When every alternative has the same kind, the list would read `unit U1 is one of these:` over a single bullet. That promises a choice the definition does not offer. So the verbalizer says it as one sentence: `unit U1 is unfounded exactly when U1 is a spec that cites no unit`.

<details>
<summary>Alloy</summary>

```alloy
all f: Definition | (f in OneKind and byKind[f]) implies f in OneSentenceKind
```

</details>

#### @spec a-definition-by-cases-is-said-as-it-stands-when-an-alternative-does-not-begin-with-its-kind

<!-- statement-spec-a-definition-by-cases-is-said-as-it-stands-when-an-alternative-does-not-begin-with-its-kind:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> When a [*definition*](#term-definition-passage) has an alternative that does not begin with its kind, the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says the definition as a list of the alternatives as they stand.
<!-- statement-spec-a-definition-by-cases-is-said-as-it-stands-when-an-alternative-does-not-begin-with-its-kind:end -->

The phrase for a kind needs a kind to head it: `a spec that …`. An alternative such as `the unit is not an axiom` names no kind, so no phrase can start with one. Forcing it into the list would drop a case or invent a kind. So when any alternative does not open with its kind, the verbalizer keeps every alternative as it stands, under `at least one of these holds`.

<details>
<summary>Alloy</summary>

```alloy
all f: Definition | f in NoKindFirst implies f in AsItStands
```

</details>

#### @spec a-definition-by-cases-is-said-as-it-stands-when-a-run-of-and-would-read-two-ways

<!-- statement-spec-a-definition-by-cases-is-said-as-it-stands-when-a-run-of-and-would-read-two-ways:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> When a [*definition*](#term-definition-passage) has a run of "and" beside another alternative of its kind, the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says the definition as a list of the alternatives as they stand.
<!-- statement-spec-a-definition-by-cases-is-said-as-it-stands-when-a-run-of-and-would-read-two-ways:end -->

Two cases of one kind merge with "or", and that breaks when one case is itself a run of "and". Then `A spec that is not tested and is not paired or cites no unit` can group the "or" two ways. It can join the last clause, or the whole run. The two groupings define different units, and nothing in the words picks one.

So the verbalizer lists the alternatives as they stand, each on its own bullet. A run of "and" that is alone in its kind stays a phrase, since no "or" meets it.

<details>
<summary>Alloy</summary>

```alloy
all f: Definition | f in AmbiguousAnd implies f in AsItStands
```

</details>

#### @spec a-definition-by-cases-is-said-as-it-stands-when-an-alternative-is-not-about-its-subject

<!-- statement-spec-a-definition-by-cases-is-said-as-it-stands-when-an-alternative-is-not-about-its-subject:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> When a [*definition*](#term-definition-passage) has an alternative that says something about another unit, the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says the definition as a list of the alternatives as they stand.
<!-- statement-spec-a-definition-by-cases-is-said-as-it-stands-when-an-alternative-is-not-about-its-subject:end -->

Each line of a definition by kinds reads `a bug that …`, so every clause after "that" must be about the bug. Term-hidden has a case `project has a tracker and the unit names no issue`. Put after "a bug that", "has a tracker" would read as a claim about the bug, not the project. So when any alternative says something of another thing, the verbalizer keeps the alternatives as they stand, each with its own subject.

<details>
<summary>Alloy</summary>

```alloy
all f: Definition | f in NotAboutSubject implies f in AsItStands
```

</details>

#### @spec a-definition-by-cases-is-said-as-it-stands-when-two-of-its-kinds-can-share-a-member

<!-- statement-spec-a-definition-by-cases-is-said-as-it-stands-when-two-of-its-kinds-can-share-a-member:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> When a [*definition*](#term-definition-passage) has two kinds that can share a member, the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says the definition as a list of the alternatives as they stand.
<!-- statement-spec-a-definition-by-cases-is-said-as-it-stands-when-two-of-its-kinds-can-share-a-member:end -->

`The unit is one of these: a spec that is tested; a bug that is paired`, and a reader can take that as exactly one line. When specs and bugs share no member, as signatures that extend one signature, nothing meets two lines and both readings agree. When a unit can be a spec and a bug at once, a tested, paired one meets both lines. A reader taking "exactly one" would then wrongly leave it out. So the verbalizer lists the alternatives as they stand, under `at least one of these holds`.

<details>
<summary>Alloy</summary>

```alloy
all f: Definition | f in KindsShareAMember implies f in AsItStands
```

</details>

#### @spec a-definition-by-cases-is-said-as-it-stands-when-an-option-of-a-kind-holds-a-comma

<!-- statement-spec-a-definition-by-cases-is-said-as-it-stands-when-an-option-of-a-kind-holds-a-comma:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> When a [*definition*](#term-definition-passage) has an option of one kind that holds a comma, the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says the definition as a list of the alternatives as they stand.
<!-- statement-spec-a-definition-by-cases-is-said-as-it-stands-when-an-option-of-a-kind-holds-a-comma:end -->

Said kind by kind, the options of one kind run after "that", joined by commas and one "or". An option that holds a comma of its own breaks that run. Take "a bug that cites a unit that is not an axiom, a spec or a bug or is not tested". Does "or is not tested" belong to the bug, or to the unit it cites? The reader cannot tell.

So the verbalizer says such a definition as it stands, each alternative on its own bullet.

<details>
<summary>Alloy</summary>

```alloy
all f: Definition | f in CommaInOption implies f in AsItStands
```

</details>

##### @bug a-kind-of-two-options-with-a-comma-is-said-as-one-run

> Where a kind has exactly two options and one holds a comma, the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says them as one run after "that", which reads two ways.

The printer says the definition as it stands only when such a kind has more than two options. The read-back check finds one meaning, because the parser does not model where the second "or" attaches.

Issue: #85

#### @spec a-word-that-names-a-term-links-to-the-unit-that-holds-its-reading-in-markdown

> In the Markdown layout, the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) links a word whose reading a unit holds to that unit.

This follows because a reader who meets the word can follow it to what it means.

#### @spec a-word-its-caller-marks-is-a-term-mark-in-markdown

> In the Markdown layout, the verbalizer writes the text of a link that its caller marks between single asterisks: `[*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer)`.

This follows because the asterisks set the word apart as a word of the canon, and the link still leads to its term. Only the caller knows which links name a term, because the verbalizer does not read the terms of a document. Every other word links as before.

#### @spec a-word-that-names-a-term-is-plain-in-the-text-layout

> In the text layout, the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says a word whose reading a unit holds in plain words.

This follows because the text layout has no way to hold a link.

#### @spec only-the-first-mention-of-a-term-links

> In a [*linked formula*](#term-linked-formula), the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) links only the first mention of a term, in reading order.

This follows because a link on every mention fills the page with blue, and the reader learns the term once.

#### @spec a-word-never-links-to-the-unit-its-sentence-is-in

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) never links a word to the unit whose statement it is saying.

This follows because a link to the page the reader is on goes nowhere.

#### @spec a-reading-that-points-at-a-unit-links-to-it

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) links a word whose reading points at a unit to that unit.

This follows because the author wrote the link by hand to name exactly where the word leads.

#### @spec a-link-in-a-table-held-in-another-document-goes-through-its-path

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) writes a link of a table held in another document, to an anchor of that document, through the path to it.

This follows because a link written as `#anchor` points into the document that holds the table, and a reader meets the words in another.

#### @spec the-nouns-of-a-quantifier-link-and-the-article-follows-the-word

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) links the noun of a quantified type whose reading a unit holds, and chooses the article by the word, not the bracket.

This follows because the variable is a thing of the type, so a reader may follow the noun. A bracket must not change a or an.

#### @spec a-sentence-starts-with-a-capital-on-the-word-and-not-on-the-bracket

> When a statement begins with a linked or marked word, the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) puts the capital on its first letter, inside the link or the mark.

This follows because the capital belongs to the first letter a reader sees.

#### @spec a-reading-held-by-no-unit-has-plain-words

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says a word whose reading no unit holds in plain words, even in the Markdown layout.

This follows because a word with no unit to lead to is only a word.

#### @spec a-variable-said-once-takes-the-place-of-its-quantifier-as-a-noun-phrase

<!-- statement-spec-a-variable-said-once-takes-the-place-of-its-quantifier-as-a-noun-phrase:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> When the sentence says the variable of a [*quantifier*](#term-quantifier) once and the quantifier [*fits*](#term-fit) a noun phrase, the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says the quantifier as a noun phrase in the place of the variable, such as "sits in no unit".
<!-- statement-spec-a-variable-said-once-takes-the-place-of-its-quantifier-as-a-noun-phrase:end -->

Spelled out in full, `some o: Owner | o in c.on` reads `there is an owner such that c is on the owner`. The reader meets the owner twice and must match the two mentions. When the sentence names the variable once and the quantifier [*fits*](#term-fit) a noun phrase, the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) puts the phrase where the variable stood: `c is on an owner`. Under "no" it reads `c is on no owner`.

<details>
<summary>Alloy</summary>

```alloy
all f: Quantifier | (f in VariableOnce and fits[f]) implies f in AsNounPhrase
```

</details>

The pass `noun-phrases` is pass 12 of 25 in the pipeline. It changes 195 of the 1776 formulas of the sweep.

The shortest of them, as written in Alloy:

```text

```

Without the pass:

```text
When there is a cleanup that is on an owner, pulse has disposed the owner.
```

With it:

```text
When a cleanup is on an owner, pulse has disposed the owner.
```

- Rejected: a noun phrase hanging only from another noun phrase, "a cleanup is on an owner": it reads as said of every cleanup.

#### @spec a-bare-noun-phrase-may-stand-inside-its-clause

> A noun phrase with "a" or "another" and no relative clause may stand inside its clause. It stands where the variable stands: "a block of another unit names the word".

This follows because a bare noun phrase ends where its noun does, so a reader takes no word after it for a part of it. A noun phrase with a relative clause still stands at the start or the end of its clause. So does one with "no": a reader could take "the author asks about leaving out no unit" for asking about leaving nothing out.

#### @spec a-noun-phrase-can-be-the-subject-of-a-sentence

<!-- statement-spec-a-noun-phrase-can-be-the-subject-of-a-sentence:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> When the variable of a [*quantifier*](#term-quantifier) is the subject of the sentence and the quantifier [*fits*](#term-fit) a noun phrase, the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says the quantifier with the noun phrase as the subject, such as "a tag names unit U1".
<!-- statement-spec-a-noun-phrase-can-be-the-subject-of-a-sentence:end -->

In `some d: Cleanup | o in d.on`, the cleanup is what the sentence is about. Spelled out, it reads `there is a cleanup such that the cleanup is on o`. When the quantifier fits a noun phrase, the phrase opens the sentence as its subject instead: `a cleanup is on o`, or `no cleanup is on o`. The o after the verb gives the phrase something to hang from.

<details>
<summary>Alloy</summary>

```alloy
all f: Quantifier | (f in VariableSubject and fits[f]) implies f in AsSubjectPhrase
```

</details>

#### @spec what-else-is-true-of-the-variable-is-a-relative-clause

<!-- statement-spec-what-else-is-true-of-the-variable-is-a-relative-clause:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> When the variable of a [*quantifier*](#term-quantifier) has a further condition and the quantifier [*fits*](#term-fit) a noun phrase, the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says the quantifier with a relative clause, such as "a unit that is a spec".
<!-- statement-spec-what-else-is-true-of-the-variable-is-a-relative-clause:end -->

`some o: Owner | o in c.on and o in Disposed` says two things of one owner. In full it reads `there is an owner such that c is on the owner and pulse has disposed the owner`. When the quantifier fits a noun phrase, the second condition joins the phrase as a relative clause: `c is on an owner that pulse has disposed`. The reader meets one owner, once.

<details>
<summary>Alloy</summary>

```alloy
all f: Quantifier | (f in VariableWithCondition and fits[f]) implies f in RelativeClause
```

</details>

#### @spec relative-clauses-that-share-their-subject-say-it-once

> Several conditions of a noun phrase may each end with its thing and share the words before their verbs. The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) then says them as one relative clause that says those words once: "an issue that the tracker knows and has not closed".

Derives from: [`axiom-a-formula-is-said-as-a-person-would-write-it`](#axiom-a-formula-is-said-as-a-person-would-write-it)

This follows because each condition says the same subject, and a person says a subject once for all its verbs. Without the shared words, the noun phrase could take one of the conditions only. The thing would then stay in a "such that" with the others.

#### @spec a-thing-after-a-preposition-is-said-with-the-preposition-and-which

> Where the thing of a relative clause stands after a preposition at the end of its reading, the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) puts the preposition before "which". So `the checker reports no finding for {1}` gives "an expected failure for which the checker reports no finding".

Derives from: [`axiom-a-formula-is-said-as-a-person-would-write-it`](#axiom-a-formula-is-said-as-a-person-would-write-it)

This follows because "that the checker reports no finding for" leaves its preposition at the end. There the reader looks for the noun it governs. The preposition then stands beside the noun it is about. A preposition is one of a few words: about, after, before, by, for, from, in, into, of, on, over, to and with.

The preposition moves only where words stand between it and the verb. So "an owner of which p is the parent", but "an owner that d is on". With the verb right before the preposition, "on which d is" would leave the verb alone at the end.

#### @spec several-negations-of-a-variable-are-one-negation

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says several negations of a variable as one negation that lists the kinds, when the [*quantifier*](#term-quantifier) [*fits*](#term-fit) a noun phrase.

This follows because "that is not an axiom, a spec or a fact" is shorter and easier to read than three negations.

#### @spec a-variable-that-must-differ-from-another-of-its-kind-is-said-as-another

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says a variable that must differ from another of its kind as "another" before the noun, when the [*quantifier*](#term-quantifier) [*fits*](#term-fit) a noun phrase.

This follows because "another unit" says what the logic compares, without a name to follow.

#### @spec a-variable-that-must-differ-from-one-value-is-said-as-other-than-it

> When the [*quantifier*](#term-quantifier) [*fits*](#term-fit) a noun phrase, the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says a variable that must differ from one value as its noun "other than" the value. The value is a variable or a string, as in "a text other than "a"". It says a variable that must differ from several values in full.

This follows because "other than" names the one value the variable is not. A phrase has room for one such value, so it would leave out a second.

#### @spec variables-of-different-kinds-nest-as-phrases

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says variables of different kinds as nested phrases, when the [*quantifier*](#term-quantifier) [*fits*](#term-fit) a noun phrase.

This follows because a test that checks a bug that sits in a unit reads from left to right.

`some o: Owner | o in o.parent` says that one owner is its own parent. As noun phrases it would read `an owner is the parent of an owner`, which a reader takes as two owners. #### @spec a-quantifier-with-nothing-to-attach-to-is-said-in-full

<!-- statement-spec-a-quantifier-with-nothing-to-attach-to-is-said-in-full:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> When all of these hold:

A noun phrase alone in its sentence misleads: `a cleanup has run` reads as a rule about every cleanup. `There is a … that` repairs most such cases, as the next spec says. Where it cannot, the verbalizer says the quantifier in full. The pass `there-is-a-that` is pass 14 of 25 in the pipeline. It changes 4 of the 1776 formulas of the sweep.

- Readers: A strict judge (Opus) found 46 of 46 changed statements lossless; two haiku readers judged 16 situations each and got all of them right.
- Readers: For the bullets after "that:", two haiku readers and one sonnet reader judged 7 situations each and got all of them right, including one list meeting some conditions and another the rest.
- Rejected: "a unit is a spec": reads as said of every unit.
- Rejected: "no claim takes no lane": a double negative.
- Rejected: bullets after "there is no unit that:": each bullet could read as denied on its own.
- Rejected: "there is a list that has three clauses or fewer, has an item that holds a comma and has more than two clauses": the relative clause "that holds a comma" can run over what follows it.

This works only when the claim is one plain line. A time phrase, a relative clause, a comma or a "when" in the claim could reach over the "when" after it. In `c is on an owner that pulse has disposed when …`, the "when" could belong to "disposed". An "otherwise" speaks of what the first side does not hold of, so such a rule keeps its first side first too. So does a rule said `from now on, whenever`, where "whenever" has taken the place of "when".

<details>
<summary>Alloy</summary>

```alloy
all f: Series | (f in ListFirstSide and f in PlainSecondSide and f not in Otherwise and f not in Whenever) implies f in SecondSideFirst
```

</details>

<!-- pass-claim-first:begin — generated by `node test/core/wordings.ts --write`; edits are overwritten -->
The pass `claim-first` is pass 22 of 25 in the pipeline. It changes 9 of the 1776 formulas of the sweep.

The shortest of them, as written in Alloy:

```text
all c: Cleanup | all o: Owner | (c in Ran and o in Disposed and o not in Stopped) implies o in c.on
```

Without the pass:

```text
When all of these hold:
  - a cleanup has run
  - pulse has disposed an owner
  - the dispose of the owner has not been stopped
then the cleanup is on the owner.
```

With it:

```text
A cleanup is on an owner when all of these hold:
  - the cleanup has run
  - pulse has disposed the owner
  - the dispose of the owner has not been stopped
```
<!-- pass-claim-first:end -->

#### @spec a-rule-that-is-a-side-of-a-rule-is-set-apart

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) sets a rule that is a side of another rule apart, below "the following holds".

This follows because a "when" inside a "when", or an "otherwise" after two of them, would not show which rule each part belongs to.

#### @spec a-first-side-that-holds-a-time-phrase-is-set-apart

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) sets the first side of a rule apart, below "when the following holds", when the side holds a time phrase.

This follows because a reader could take the time phrase as covering the second side too, even when "then" starts a line of its own.

#### @spec a-side-that-holds-a-comma-is-set-apart-where-no-then-marks-the-second-side

> When a rule would stand on one line with no "then", the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) sets apart a side with a comma of its own. When both sides hold one, it sets the second side apart.

This follows because the comma would read as where the second side starts. On one line, "then" stands only before a time phrase. In "when r, a, and at the next moment, b", a reader could put "a" in the first side.

#### @spec a-condition-that-is-a-series-is-said-as-a-list

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) sets apart a condition that is a [*series*](#term-series) of clauses, "a, b and c", as a list with one clause to a line.

This follows because the comma of a series in a condition would read as the end of the condition. A list ends where its last item does, and puts each clause on a line of its own.

#### @spec a-comma-of-a-reading-after-then-is-left-on-its-line

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) leaves on its line a second side whose only comma is inside the words of a reading, such as ", such as …" or ", with …".

This follows because a comma inside a reading is the author's and ends with the reading. A reader cannot take it as the end of the condition, which ended at the comma before. A reading's comma in the first side is still set apart.

#### @spec a-second-side-that-holds-a-time-phrase-before-an-otherwise-is-set-apart

> In a rule with an "otherwise", the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) sets the second side apart when it holds a time phrase, the one it begins with included.

This follows because a reader could take the time phrase as covering the "otherwise" too.

#### @spec a-second-or-last-side-of-a-rule-that-holds-a-series-is-set-apart

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) sets apart a side of a rule after "then" or "otherwise" when that side is a [*series*](#term-series) of clauses after a comma.

This follows because a reader could take the last clause of the series as a claim of its own, outside the rule. An example is "a, and at the next moment, b".

## @axiom a-formula-is-said-as-a-person-would-write-it

> Among the words that say a [*formula*](#term-formula) without loss, the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says the ones a person would write. Those are sentences before bullets, each thing named once, and the fewest words that still say it all. It uses only the turns of English that the reading rules settle, so that no reader has to guess what a sentence means.

This follows because more people read a statement than write it, and stiff words cost each reader time. A reader who has to work out which clause a phrase belongs to may also work it out wrong.

The [*frame*](#term-frame) of each reading tells the verbalizer which of those turns a reading can take.

The axiom ranks below [`axiom-a-formula-is-said-without-loss`](#axiom-a-formula-is-said-without-loss). Where the two pull apart, a loss is refused before a stiff phrase is. So fluency goes only as far as a rule of [`axiom-a-short-list-of-rules-settles-what-english-leaves-open`](#axiom-a-short-list-of-rules-settles-what-english-leaves-open) pins it down. A turn of English that readers do not apply the same way each time, such as which noun a trailing clause belongs to, stays out. The words fall back to bullets there.

### @spec each-thing-of-a-rule-over-several-is-said-as-every-and-its-conditions

> Take a "for every" over several things, whose rule has no "otherwise" and holds no other quantifier. Its first side says only conditions that each name one of the things, at least one for each. Its second side is one clause that names each thing once. The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says that clause with each thing as "every", its noun, and its conditions as a relative clause. So the passes read "every pass that moves a negation inward runs before every pass that says a quantifier as a noun phrase".

This follows because a person states a rule over two kinds of thing this way. "For every pass P1 and every pass P2" names the passes twice, numbers them, and puts their conditions apart from the clause they matter to.

Two "every" in one clause leave a reader no order to get wrong. Every pass and every pass is the same claim either way round. A rule that holds another quantifier stays as it was. An "every" beside an "a" or a "no" has two orders a reader could take.

<!-- pass-every-phrases:begin — generated by `node test/core/wordings.ts --write`; edits are overwritten -->
The pass `every-phrases` is pass 7 of 25 in the pipeline. It changes 1 of the 1776 formulas of the sweep.

The shortest of them, as written in Alloy:

```text
all c: Cleanup, o: Owner | (c in Ran and o in Disposed) implies o in c.on
```

Without the pass:

```text
When a cleanup has run and pulse has disposed an owner, the cleanup is on the owner.
```

With it:

```text
Every cleanup that has run is on every owner that pulse has disposed.
```
<!-- pass-every-phrases:end -->

### @spec a-thing-only-the-first-side-of-a-rule-names-is-said-there-as-a-noun-phrase

> Take a "for every" whose rule names a thing in its first side alone. The clauses there that name the thing may make a noun phrase of it. The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) then says the thing in that side as that noun phrase. So a rule over two units and a word opens "when a block of another unit names the word outside its declaration".

This follows because a rule for every such thing says that its second side holds wherever some such thing makes its first side hold. The words then need the thing only where it matters, and the "for every" names it no more.

The thing stays in the "for every" where another thing of its kind stays there too. Only a thing that must differ from that one may go. "When a cleanup is on an owner and a cleanup is on the owner" leaves the reader to wonder if the two cleanups are one. "Another unit" says they are not.

<!-- pass-some-in-when:begin — generated by `node test/core/wordings.ts --write`; edits are overwritten -->
The pass `some-in-when` is pass 11 of 25 in the pipeline. It changes 35 of the 1776 formulas of the sweep.

The shortest of them, as written in Alloy:

```text
all c: Cleanup, o: Owner | o in c.on implies o in Disposed
```

Without the pass:

```text
For every cleanup and every owner:
  when the cleanup is on the owner, pulse has disposed the owner.
```

With it:

```text
When a cleanup is on an owner, pulse has disposed the owner.
```
<!-- pass-some-in-when:end -->

### @spec a-thing-of-a-some-is-said-inside-the-clauses-that-name-it

> Take a "some" over several things, and a thing of it that only some of its clauses name. Where those clauses say a noun phrase of the thing, the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) says the thing inside them. So `some d: Document, u: Unit | d in Worded and d->u in Hold.units and u in Logical` reads "a document that keeps readings and holds a unit that holds a formula".

This follows because a person names each thing once, where it first matters, and says what holds of it there. A "for some" above a list of bullets names each thing again in every bullet. The thing moves only where its clauses make a noun phrase. Elsewhere the words would nest one "such that" in another, which reads no better than the list.

It moves only where two clauses or more name it, so that the noun phrase says more of it than the clause that links it. A bare "an owner" saves no clause, and a reader could take a later "and has run" for a clause of the owner. A "some" that the [noun phrases](#spec-a-variable-said-once-takes-the-place-of-its-quantifier-as-a-noun-phrase) already say whole keeps the order they give it.

The clause that holds the noun phrase comes after the other clauses of the "some". A reader could take a clause after it for part of its relative clause.

A thing that must differ from another stays too. "Another owner" differs from the owner named last before it, and moving the thing would change which owner that is. Two things of a kind that must differ from each other move together, where their clauses then say "a … and another …": "the conflict names a unit and names another unit".

<!-- pass-some-inside:begin — generated by `node test/core/wordings.ts --write`; edits are overwritten -->
The pass `some-inside` is pass 10 of 25 in the pipeline. It changes 6 of the 1776 formulas of the sweep.

The shortest of them, as written in Alloy:

```text
some c: Cleanup, o: Owner | c in Ran and o in c.on and o in Disposed
```

Without the pass:

```text
For some cleanup and some owner:
  the cleanup has run, is on the owner and pulse has disposed the owner.
```

With it:

```text
There is a cleanup that has run and is on an owner that pulse has disposed.
```
<!-- pass-some-inside:end -->

### @spec a-reading-gives-its-frame-by-a-marked-verb

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) reads the word of a reading between carets as its verb, which gives the reading its [*frame*](#term-frame).

This follows because a relative clause, a passive and a negative each change the words around the verb. The verb is where the words of a reading turn. The verbalizer needs to know where it stands to say any of these.

#### @spec a-mark-is-no-part-of-the-words-of-a-reading

> The carets of a mark are no part of the words of a reading: `{1} ^keeps^ readings` reads "keeps readings".

This follows because the mark is for the verbalizer, and the reader sees the words alone.

#### @spec a-verb-line-gives-the-forms-of-a-marked-verb

> A line `verb keeps: keep, kept` of the readings gives the marked verb `keeps` its infinitive `keep` and its participle `kept`.

This follows because the verbalizer inflects no word itself. A rule of English would say "keeped".

#### @spec a-verb-line-wins-over-a-standard-verb

> A `verb` line of the readings gives the forms of its verb in place of those of the [*standard verb*](#term-standard-verb) it spells.

This follows because a canon may use a verb in a sense of its own, and the nearer words count most.

#### @spec the-standard-verbs-are-the-verb-terms-of-verbs-md

> The [*standard verbs*](#term-standard-verb) are the verb terms of [VERBS.md](VERBS.md). Each gives its third person and its participle in its grammar table, and its stem is its infinitive.

This follows because a standard verb is a word, and a canon defines a word as a term: what it means, and its forms. A script writes the list in the source from the terms, and a test fails where the two differ.

#### @spec a-standard-verb-needs-no-verb-line

> A reading may mark a [*standard verb*](#term-standard-verb) with no `verb` line for it, and takes its forms from naturalloy.

This follows because most readings use common verbs, and a canon should not list the forms of "holds" again.

#### @spec a-reading-with-no-negative-side-takes-the-negative-of-its-frame

> Where a reading marks its verb and gives no negative side, its negative is its positive with one change at the verb:
> - "is" becomes "is not", and "are" becomes "are not"
> - any other verb becomes "does not" and its infinitive: `{1} ^keeps^ readings` gives `{1} does not keep readings`

This follows because a negative that says the positive with "not" at its verb says exactly that the positive does not hold. The author writes a negative only where another one reads better, such as "keeps no readings".

#### @spec a-reading-whose-negative-its-frame-cannot-give-is-refused

> The [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) refuses a line of readings that gives no negative side and marks a verb that:
> - is not "is" or "are"
> - has no `verb` line that gives its infinitive
> - is no [*standard verb*](#term-standard-verb)

This follows because a negative the verbalizer had to guess could say something else than the positive does not hold. The refusal names the verb.

## @thread a-statement-could-be-said-in-tiers-from-its-ir

Since the verbalizer holds the IR of each formula, it could say a statement in more than one tier. The checked statement would stay lossless under the reading rules. Beside it, a looser tier could read the way a person writes, marked as such, and never the claim. The owner of the design chose the single lossless tier for now, and left the tiers for later.

## @axiom a-short-list-of-rules-settles-what-english-leaves-open

> A short [*list*](#term-series) of rules settles what English leaves open, so that each statement means only what its [*formula*](#term-formula) means.

English leaves some things open that a formula fixes: where a phrase stops, which noun a "that" follows, and from when "now" counts. The verbalizer settles each of these one way, and the rules below say which. A reader learns them once. A probe can then ask whether readers really read that way. Attempto Controlled English keeps such rules for the same reason.

#### @spec a-noun-phrase-covers-the-clause-it-stands-in

> A noun phrase says its [*quantifier*](#term-quantifier) over the clause it stands in, and over nothing beyond it. "The cleanup is on no owner" says that no owner has the cleanup on it.

This follows because the clause is the smallest stretch of words that holds the noun phrase. A reader looks no further for what it covers.

#### @spec every-and-a-relative-clause-stands-for-each-thing-the-clause-holds-of

> "Every pass that moves a negation inward" stands for each pass of which its relative clause holds. The clause it stands in says its claim of each such pass.

This follows because "every" in English speaks of each thing of its kind, and the relative clause narrows the kind. A clause with two such phrases says its claim of each pair.

#### @spec the-first-noun-phrase-of-a-clause-covers-the-next

> Of two noun phrases in one clause, the first covers the second. "No cleanup is on an owner" says that no cleanup is on any owner.

This follows because a reader meets the first phrase first, and takes what follows as said of what it names.

#### @spec a-relative-clause-says-more-of-the-noun-it-follows

> A relative clause, "that …" or a preposition and "which …", says what else holds of the noun right before it. An "and" inside it joins only its own conditions.

This follows because "that" points back to the nearest noun. The verbalizer puts a relative clause only where nothing follows that its "and" could take in. In "an issue that the tracker knows and has not closed", the words after "and" take the subject that the first condition gives, "the tracker".

#### @spec the-noun-alone-names-the-one-thing-of-its-kind

> "The cleanup" names the one cleanup the statement speaks of. Where two things of one kind are in play, each keeps its number, as "cleanup_1" and "cleanup_2" do.

This follows because "the" picks out one thing, and a reader can tell which one only when one thing of that kind is in play.

#### @spec now-is-the-moment-a-statement-is-read-at

> "Now" is the moment a reader takes the statement at. Inside "from now on" or "at the next moment", it is each moment that phrase picks.

This follows because a time phrase moves the reader to the moments it names, and the words below it hold there.

#### @spec a-time-phrase-covers-the-rest-of-its-sentence

> A time phrase covers the words after it up to the end of its sentence. Where it ends in a colon, it covers the lines set apart below it.

This follows because a reader has no other mark of where a time phrase stops. So the verbalizer sets apart below it any words with a time phrase of their own.

#### @spec until-then-stops-before-its-moment

> "b now or later, and until then, a" says that b holds at some moment from now on. It says that a holds at every moment from now up to that one, and maybe not at it.

This follows because "until then" ends where "then" starts, as "I wait until five" does. Any moment of b gives the same truth, so the words need not say the first. On timelines built to catch each misreading, five of five readers took it this way.

#### @spec the-bullets-below-a-colon-are-the-parts-of-its-line

> The bullets below a line that ends in a colon are the parts of what that line says. Their indentation shows which line they belong to.

This follows because a list ends where its last item does, so no part of it can read as more of another.

#### @spec a-sentence-joins-its-clauses-with-and-or-with-or-never-both

> A sentence joins its clauses with "and" or with "or", and never with both. A [*list*](#term-series) shows how such clauses group.

This follows because "a and b or c" groups two ways, and a reader cannot tell which one the formula holds.

#### @spec exactly-when-goes-both-ways-and-when-goes-one

> "x exactly when y" says that each holds where the other does. "When x, y" says that y holds wherever x does, and nothing of the moments without x.

This follows because a reader takes "when" as a rule and "exactly when" as both ways. "The light is on exactly when the switch is down" reads so.

#### @spec another-differs-from-the-thing-of-its-kind-named-last

> "Another unit" and "no other unit" differ from the unit the words named last before them. That unit is in the same clause, in the clause before it, or where a [*quantifier*](#term-quantifier) introduced it.

This follows because a reader looks back for what "other" points at, as for "the". A subject that a series leaves out is not in the words, so it is not what a reader finds.

#### @spec one-of-these-names-one-of-kinds-that-share-no-member

> "x is one of these:" says that x is what one of the phrases below it names. The phrases name kinds that share no member, so x is never two of them.

This follows because "one of these" leaves open whether x may be more than one of them. Kinds that share no member settle it: "one" and "at least one" then say the same, so a reader is right either way.

#### @spec a-noun-the-words-name-again-in-a-when-is-every-thing-of-its-kind

> "A bug" stands for every bug where "the bug" follows it, in the first side of a rule or as the subject of "exactly when". "When a bug has run, code has registered the bug" says that of each bug. Two such nouns in one first side stand for every pair. "When a run asks for a command, the run exits" says that of each run and each command.

This follows because in English, "a" in a "when" speaks of whichever thing meets the condition. "The bug" after it points back at that thing, so the rule holds of each bug.

#### @spec a-claim-before-when-holds-where-the-bullets-after-it-hold

> "Code has registered a cleanup when …", followed by bullets, says what "when …, then code has registered the cleanup" says. "A cleanup" in the claim stands for every cleanup where "the cleanup" follows it in the bullets. So does each other noun that the claim says that way.

This follows because in English, a claim before "when" holds wherever what follows "when" holds. The bullets end the statement, so the "when" covers each of them. "A cleanup" there speaks of whichever cleanup the bullets go on to describe, as "a" in the first side of a rule does.

#### @spec each-statement-reads-back-to-its-meaning

> Read by these rules, the words of each statement have one meaning, and it is the meaning of what the [*verbalizer*](#term-verbalizer) said.

This follows because the rules are only of use if they settle each statement one way. A parser reads the words of the sweep back by the rules, the words of its definitions too. It finds one reading for each statement, and that reading means what the printed IR means.

#### @spec each-fixed-word-of-the-printer-reads-back-to-its-meaning

> Each fixed word of the printer stands in a statement that reads back to its one meaning. These are the intros of its lists, its time phrases, the parts of `until` and `since`, and the words of rules and of comparisons.

This follows because the sweep reads back only what its formulas happen to reach. The parser reads a fixed word that no statement holds by a rule that nothing checks. Each fixed word has a statement of its own here, so the test reads back a word the printer gains from the start.
